rules.check_logic: Check if V = I * R in the solution and ensure the material is specified as ohmic. If the resistance varies with current or temperature, Ohm's Law cannot be applied directly.
common_errors: Assuming Ohm's Law applies to non-ohmic materials (e.g., diodes, transistors)
Incorrect rearrangement of the equation (e.g., using R = V * I instead of R = V / I)

rules.title: Validate Use of Resistance Formula
rules.description: The resistance of a uniform conductor is R = ρ * (L/A), where ρ is resistivity, L is length, and A is cross-sectional area. This formula applies to uniform, isotropic materials.
rules.check_logic: Verify if R is calculated as R = ρ * (L/A), and check that all variables are properly defined and used. Ensure the conductor is uniform and isotropic.
common_errors: Forgetting to include the cross-sectional area (A) in the denominator
Using incorrect units for resistivity, length, or area
Applying this formula to non-uniform or anisotropic materials

rules.title: Check Sign Convention for Current Direction
rules.description: Current direction is conventionally defined as the flow of positive charge. It is opposite to the direction of electron flow. Ensure that the chosen current direction is consistent throughout the solution.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the current direction matches the problem setup or stated assumptions. If using electron flow, ensure it is explicitly noted.
common_errors: Confusing the direction of electron flow with conventional current
Inconsistently assigning current direction in circuit diagrams

rules.title: Verify Power Dissipation Equation
rules.description: The power dissipated in a resistor is given by P = IV, P = I^2R, or P = V^2/R, depending on the known quantities. These are derived from Ohm's Law.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the correct power formula is used based on the available variables (I, V, R). Verify the consistency of dimensional units in the power calculation.
common_errors: Using the wrong power formula for the given variables
Forgetting to square the current or voltage when using P = I^2R or P = V^2/R
Unit mismatch, such as not converting milliamps to amps

rules.title: Apply Kirchhoff's Voltage and Current Laws
rules.description: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL): The sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving it. Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL): The sum of voltage drops in a closed loop equals zero.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all currents at a junction satisfy KCL and all voltage drops around a loop satisfy KVL. Ensure consistent sign conventions for current and voltage.
common_errors: Missing terms in the summation for KCL or KVL
Incorrect sign convention for voltage drops or current directions
Failure to account for all branches in a circuit

rules.title: Ensure Dimensional Consistency in Equations
rules.description: Verify that all terms in the equations for current, resistance, voltage, and power have consistent units. For example, voltage (V) in volts, resistance (R) in ohms, current (I) in amperes, and power (P) in watts.
rules.check_logic: Check that units are consistent and correctly converted where necessary. For example, ensure that milliamps are converted to amps if necessary, and resistances in kilohms are converted to ohms.
common_errors: Using mixed units (e.g., milliamps with ohms without conversion)
Incorrect conversion of prefixes like milli, kilo, or mega
Omitting unit conversions entirely

rules.title: Verify Resistance Dependence on Temperature
rules.description: The resistance of a material changes with temperature, typically modeled as R(T) = R_0[1 + α(T - T_0)], where α is the temperature coefficient of resistance. This is crucial for non-room-temperature conditions.
rules.check_logic: Check if temperature dependence is accounted for when the problem involves significant temperature changes or explicitly mentions temperature effects.
common_errors: Ignoring the temperature dependence of resistance when significant
Using an incorrect value for the temperature coefficient (α)
Assuming resistance is constant without justification

rules.title: Check Circuit Boundary Conditions
rules.description: Ensure that all boundary conditions, such as total supplied voltage, current, or resistance, are satisfied for the entire circuit. Verify the sum of all branch currents matches the total current for parallel circuits, and total resistance is computed correctly.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the total voltage across a series circuit equals the sum of individual voltage drops, and the current splits correctly in parallel circuits.
common_errors: Incorrectly summing resistances for parallel or series configurations
Ignoring total supplied voltage or current constraints
Misapplying current or voltage division rules

rules.title: Apply Superposition Theorem
rules.description: The superposition theorem states that in a linear circuit with multiple sources, the current or voltage at any element is the algebraic sum of the currents or voltages produced by each source independently.
rules.check_logic: Verify that each independent current or voltage source is considered one at a time, with all other sources turned off (replacing voltage sources with short circuits and current sources with open circuits). Then, check that the results for each source are summed to find the total response.
common_errors: Forgetting to turn off sources aside from the one being considered
Incorrectly replacing sources (e.g., using open circuit for voltage source)
Failing to sum individual contributions correctly

rules.title: Ensure sum of voltages in a closed loop equals zero
rules.description: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) states that the algebraic sum of all voltages around a closed loop in a circuit must equal zero. This is derived from the conservation of energy principle in electrical circuits.
rules.check_logic: Sum of voltage drops and gains across all components in a closed loop must equal zero: ΣV = 0.
common_errors: Forgetting to include the polarity of voltage sources or resistors
Incorrectly summing voltage drops (e.g., forgetting negative signs for voltage drops)
Omitting a component in the loop equation

rules.title: Ensure sum of currents at a junction is zero
rules.description: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) states that the total current entering a junction must equal the total current leaving the junction. This follows from the conservation of electric charge.
rules.check_logic: Sum of currents entering and leaving a junction must be zero: ΣI_in = ΣI_out.
common_errors: Mislabeling the direction of currents at a junction
Neglecting to include all branches connected to a junction
Incorrect signs for current entering or leaving

rules.title: Verify Ohm's Law for resistive components
rules.description: Ohm's Law states that the voltage across a resistor is directly proportional to the current flowing through it: V = IR.
rules.check_logic: For each resistive component, check if V = IR holds true.
common_errors: Using incorrect resistance values from the problem statement
Forgetting to account for series or parallel combinations of resistors
Incorrect unit conversion (e.g., kilo-ohms to ohms)

rules.title: Ensure correct resistor combination rules are applied
rules.description: Resistors in series add directly (R_eq = R1 + R2 + ...), while resistors in parallel combine as reciprocals (1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...).
rules.check_logic: Check if equivalent resistance calculations for series or parallel combinations are correct.
common_errors: Using series formula for parallel resistors or vice versa
Forgetting to take the reciprocal when calculating equivalent resistance for parallel resistors
Misidentifying which resistors are in series or parallel

rules.title: Ensure power conservation in the circuit
rules.description: The total power supplied by voltage sources must equal the total power dissipated by resistors and other elements in the circuit.
rules.check_logic: Sum of power supplied (ΣP_supply = ΣV_source * I) must equal sum of power dissipated (ΣP_dissipated = ΣI^2 * R).
common_errors: Forgetting to square the current in power dissipation calculation
Misapplying the power formula for voltage sources
Ignoring power contributions from all elements in the circuit

rules.title: Verify proper sign convention usage for voltages and currents
rules.description: When applying KVL or Ohm's Law, the sign of the voltage drop or current must be consistent with the chosen direction of traversal or assumed current flow.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that voltage drops across resistors are consistent with the assumed current direction and that voltage gains are correctly identified.
common_errors: Incorrectly assigning signs to voltage drops or gains
Using inconsistent current directions for different components
Forgetting to reverse signs when changing the traversal direction in a loop

rules.title: Check for dimensional and unit consistency
rules.description: All equations involving voltages, currents, resistances, and powers must have consistent units: volts (V), amperes (A), ohms (Ω), and watts (W).
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the units in all calculations are consistent and correctly converted if necessary.
common_errors: Mixing up units (e.g., using kilo-ohms instead of ohms without proper conversion)
Using incorrect prefixes for units (e.g., mA instead of A)
Failing to check unit consistency in derived quantities like power (P = VI)

rules.title: Ensure the validity of Kirchhoff's Laws
rules.description: Kirchhoff's Laws are valid only for circuits with steady-state currents (DC circuits) and lumped elements. They cannot be applied directly to circuits with high-frequency AC signals or distributed elements like transmission lines.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the circuit operates under DC conditions and consists of lumped elements.
common_errors: Applying Kirchhoff's Laws to circuits with high-frequency AC signals
Ignoring the distributed nature of components in non-lumped systems
Using Kirchhoff's Laws in non-steady-state conditions

rules.title: Verify Ohm's Law for AC Circuits
rules.description: In AC circuits, Ohm's Law is extended to use impedance (Z) instead of resistance (R). The voltage across an element is V = I * Z, where Z can be complex.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the voltage (V) is calculated as the product of current (I) and impedance (Z). Verify that Z is expressed as a complex number in either rectangular form (R + jX) or polar form (|Z|∠θ). Confirm that the phase relationship between voltage and current is consistent with the impedance angle.
common_errors: Using resistance (R) instead of impedance (Z) in AC circuits.
Ignoring the phase angle when using complex impedance.
Incorrect conversion between polar and rectangular forms of impedance.

rules.title: Check Frequency Dependence of Reactance
rules.description: The reactance of capacitors and inductors depends on the angular frequency (ω = 2πf). Capacitive reactance is X_C = -1/(ωC), and inductive reactance is X_L = ωL.
rules.check_logic: Verify the correct formula for X_C and X_L, ensuring that the angular frequency (ω) and the element values (C or L) are used appropriately. Confirm that the negative sign is applied for capacitive reactance and that the units of reactance are in ohms (Ω).
common_errors: Using linear frequency (f) instead of angular frequency (ω = 2πf).
Incorrectly applying the negative sign for capacitive reactance.
Swapping the formulas for X_C and X_L.

rules.title: Validate Impedance in Series and Parallel Combinations
rules.description: For series circuits, impedances add directly (Z_eq = Z_1 + Z_2 + ...). For parallel circuits, the reciprocal rule applies (1/Z_eq = 1/Z_1 + 1/Z_2 + ...).
rules.check_logic: Check if the correct formulas are used for combining impedances in series and parallel configurations. Ensure proper handling of complex arithmetic, including addition, reciprocals, and conversions between polar and rectangular forms.
common_errors: Incorrectly adding impedances in parallel circuits.
Forgetting to invert the result when calculating equivalent impedance for parallel circuits.
Neglecting the imaginary component when combining impedances.

rules.title: Verify Power Calculations in AC Circuits
rules.description: The real power (P), reactive power (Q), and apparent power (S) are related to the voltage, current, and impedance phase angle: P = VIcosθ, Q = VIsinθ, and S = VI.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the correct trigonometric components of the phase angle are used to calculate P, Q, and S. Confirm that the power factor (cosθ) is consistent with the impedance angle. Verify that the units of power are consistent (watts for P, VAR for Q, and VA for S).
common_errors: Confusing real power (P) with apparent power (S).
Using incorrect trigonometric functions for P and Q.
Ignoring the phase angle in power factor calculations.

rules.title: Check Resonance Condition in RLC Circuits
rules.description: In an RLC circuit, resonance occurs when the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance (X_L = |X_C|). At resonance, the total impedance is purely resistive.
rules.check_logic: Verify that ω_res = 1/√(LC) is used to calculate the resonance angular frequency. Confirm that at resonance, Z = R (no imaginary component). Ensure that the phase angle of the impedance is zero at resonance.
common_errors: Forgetting to equalize X_L and X_C at resonance.
Misinterpreting resonance as a condition where Z = 0.
Incorrect calculation of resonance frequency using ω_res = 1/√(LC).

rules.title: Ensure Dimensional Consistency of Impedance and Reactance
rules.description: Impedance (Z) and reactance (X_L, X_C) must have the dimension of ohms (Ω). Impedance is a complex quantity, but its magnitude and components must be dimensionally consistent.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all calculations involving Z, X_L, and X_C result in units of ohms (Ω). Check the dimensional consistency of intermediate terms, such as ωL and 1/(ωC). Ensure that capacitance (C) and inductance (L) are expressed in standard units (farads and henries, respectively).
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for capacitance (C) or inductance (L).
Calculating Z or X without confirming units of intermediate terms.
Mixing incompatible units, such as radians and degrees, in calculations.

rules.title: Verify Use of RMS Values for AC Voltage and Current
rules.description: In AC circuits, root mean square (RMS) values are used for voltage and current in power and impedance calculations. RMS values relate to peak values as V_RMS = V_peak / √2 and I_RMS = I_peak / √2.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that RMS values are used in calculations unless specified otherwise. For peak values given, confirm conversion to RMS using the correct formula. Verify that RMS values are used consistently in power and impedance calculations.
common_errors: Using peak values instead of RMS values in power calculations.
Incorrect conversion between peak and RMS values.
Assuming equivalence of RMS and peak values.

rules.title: Verify Phase Angle Sign Convention
rules.description: The phase angle (θ) of impedance is positive for inductive circuits (current lags voltage) and negative for capacitive circuits (current leads voltage).
rules.check_logic: Check if the sign of the phase angle is consistent with the type of reactance (inductive or capacitive). Ensure that angles are measured in the correct unit (radians or degrees) and that conversions between units are accurate.
common_errors: Reversing the sign of the phase angle for inductive or capacitive circuits.
Using degrees and radians interchangeably without conversion.
Incorrectly interpreting the relationship between current and voltage phase.

rules.title: Verify Quality Factor in RLC Circuits
rules.description: The quality factor (Q) of an RLC circuit is a measure of its sharpness of resonance and is defined as Q = ω_resL/R for series circuits or Q = R/(ω_resL) for parallel circuits.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the correct formula for Q is used based on the circuit configuration (series or parallel). Verify that ω_res is calculated correctly and that the units of Q are dimensionless.
common_errors: Using the wrong formula for Q based on circuit configuration.
Incorrect calculation of ω_res.
Confusing the quality factor with other parameters like power factor.

rules.title: Verify Lorentz Force Equation Application
rules.description: The Lorentz force equation, F = q(E + v × B), applies to a charged particle moving in electric and magnetic fields. It calculates the force on the particle due to these fields.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the force is calculated as the vector sum of qE (electric force) and q(v × B) (magnetic force). Verify that the cross product is calculated correctly and that the electric and magnetic contributions are combined as vectors.
common_errors: Omitting one of the terms (qE or q(v × B)).
Using scalar multiplication instead of the vector cross product for v × B.
Incorrectly calculating the direction of the cross product using the right-hand rule.

rules.title: Check Dimensional Consistency for Magnetic Field Units
rules.description: The magnetic field (B) is measured in Tesla (T), which is equivalent to N/(A·m). Ensure calculations respect these units and are dimensionally consistent.
rules.check_logic: Verify that B is derived or expressed in consistent units, and that related physical quantities (force, velocity, charge, etc.) align dimensionally. Ensure that derived units are converted correctly when necessary.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for B, e.g., treating it as a scalar without units.
Failure to include the current (A) factor when converting derived units.
Mixing up units for related quantities like force or velocity.

rules.title: Ensure Use of Right-Hand Rule for Cross Products
rules.description: The direction of the magnetic force (q(v × B)) is determined using the right-hand rule: point fingers along v, curl toward B, and thumb gives the force direction for a positive charge.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the cross product direction is determined correctly using the right-hand rule for the given vectors. Ensure the rule is reversed for negative charges.
common_errors: Using the left-hand rule instead of the right-hand rule.
Incorrectly swapping the order of v and B in the cross product (v × B ≠ B × v).
Forgetting to reverse the direction for negative charges.

rules.title: Check Magnetic Force Does No Work
rules.description: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity of the charged particle, meaning it does no work (W = F · d = 0).
rules.check_logic: Verify that the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity vector (v · F = 0), and ensure no work is calculated for it. Confirm that any work done is attributed to other forces, such as the electric force.
common_errors: Incorrectly assuming the magnetic force does work on the particle.
Failing to check the orthogonality of v and F.
Misattributing work done by other forces to the magnetic force.

rules.title: Verify Consistency in Coordinate System Orientation
rules.description: Magnetic fields and forces often involve three-dimensional vector calculations. Ensure the coordinate system used follows a right-handed convention.
rules.check_logic: Check that the coordinate axes follow the right-hand rule (x × y = z). Verify that all vector calculations are consistent with this orientation.
common_errors: Using a left-handed coordinate system.
Mixing up coordinate axes when calculating cross products.
Failing to verify the orientation of the coordinate system in complex setups.

rules.title: Ensure Correct Radius for Circular Motion in Magnetic Fields
rules.description: For a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field, the magnetic force provides centripetal acceleration. The radius is r = mv/(qB).
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the radius is calculated using r = mv/(qB), with the direction of the motion forming a circle perpendicular to the magnetic field. Verify that the velocity is perpendicular to the magnetic field for circular motion.
common_errors: Using incorrect formulas for radius.
Forgetting velocity must be perpendicular to the magnetic field for circular motion.
Ignoring the charge sign when determining motion direction.

rules.title: Check Validity for Static Charges
rules.description: The Lorentz force equation does not apply to static charges since v = 0 eliminates the magnetic force (q(v × B) = 0).
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the velocity is non-zero if applying the magnetic force component of the Lorentz force equation. Verify that only the electric force qE acts on a stationary charge.
common_errors: Applying q(v × B) to static charges.
Failing to recognize that only the electric force qE acts on a stationary charge.

rules.title: Verify Conditions for Biot-Savart Law Application
rules.description: The Biot-Savart law calculates the magnetic field B due to a current element. It applies to steady currents and must integrate over the entire current distribution.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the current is steady and the law is applied to infinitesimal current elements (dL) before integrating. Verify that the contributions from all current elements are summed correctly.
common_errors: Applying the Biot-Savart law to time-varying currents.
Failing to integrate over the entire current distribution.
Incorrectly calculating the vector contributions (direction or magnitude) from each current element.

rules.title: Verify Application of Ampere's Circuital Law
rules.description: Ampere's circuital law relates the line integral of the magnetic field around a closed loop to the current passing through the loop (∮B·dl = μ₀I).
rules.check_logic: Ensure the law is applied to closed loops and that the current enclosed by the loop is correctly calculated. Verify that the magnetic field is tangential to the loop at every point.
common_errors: Applying the law to open loops.
Incorrectly calculating the enclosed current.
Failing to account for symmetry when simplifying the integral.

rules.title: Verify Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law Application
rules.description: Faraday's law states that a changing magnetic flux induces an electromotive force (EMF), and Lenz's law determines the direction of the induced current (EMF = -dΦ/dt).
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the EMF is calculated as the negative rate of change of magnetic flux. Verify that the induced current opposes the change in flux, consistent with Lenz's law.
common_errors: Ignoring the negative sign in Faraday's law.
Incorrectly determining the direction of the induced current.
Failing to account for all contributions to the changing flux.

rules.title: Verify correct application of Biot-Savart Law equation
rules.description: The Biot-Savart Law states that the magnetic field dB at a point due to a current element I·dl is proportional to the cross product of the current element vector and the unit vector pointing from the current element to the observation point, divided by the square of the distance between them. This law is given as: dB = (μ₀ / 4π) * (I·dl × r̂) / r². It applies for steady currents.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the magnetic field contribution dB is calculated using the cross product (I·dl × r̂), and the denominator contains r² where r is the distance between the current element and the observation point. Verify that μ₀ / 4π is included as a constant multiplier.
common_errors: Forgetting to include the cross product in the equation
Incorrectly calculating the distance r or the unit vector r̂
Omitting the constant μ₀ / 4π
Using r instead of r² in the denominator
Using non-steady currents, which invalidates the law

rules.title: Verify correct application of Ampere's Law in integral form
rules.description: Ampere's Law relates the closed line integral of the magnetic field B around a closed loop to the current enclosed by the loop: ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enclosed. It is valid for steady currents and symmetric geometries where the magnetic field is uniform along the loop.
rules.check_logic: Check if the line integral of B·dl is properly calculated and equated to μ₀ times the total current enclosed by the loop. Ensure the loop is chosen to align with the symmetry of the problem.
common_errors: Failure to consider the direction of the magnetic field (sign convention in B·dl)
Forgetting to enclose the current completely within the loop
Applying Ampere's Law to non-steady currents
Incorrectly assuming symmetry in situations where it does not exist

rules.title: Ensure correct use of coordinate systems and sign conventions
rules.description: Both Biot-Savart Law and Ampere's Law require consistent application of coordinate systems (Cartesian, cylindrical, or spherical) to define vectors. The right-hand rule is used to determine the direction of the magnetic field.
rules.check_logic: Verify the coordinate system used is consistent throughout the problem, and the right-hand rule is applied correctly for cross products and determining field directions. Ensure proper transformations are applied when switching between coordinate systems.
common_errors: Switching between coordinate systems without proper transformations
Incorrect application of the right-hand rule for the cross product
Mislabeling components of vectors in the chosen system

rules.title: Verify geometric constraints for symmetry in Ampere's Law
rules.description: Ampere's Law in integral form is most effective for symmetric geometries like infinite wires, solenoids, or toroids, where the magnetic field is uniform and constant around the chosen loop.
rules.check_logic: Check if the geometry satisfies symmetry conditions. For instance, ensure the magnetic field is constant along the loop or the current enclosed is distributed uniformly. Verify that the chosen Amperian loop aligns with the geometry.
common_errors: Applying Ampere's Law to asymmetric geometries
Neglecting to account for non-uniformity in the magnetic field
Incorrectly selecting an Amperian loop that does not align with the geometry

rules.title: Ensure laws are applied to steady currents only
rules.description: Both Biot-Savart Law and Ampere's Law are valid only for steady (time-independent) currents. For time-varying currents, Maxwell's equations, including the displacement current, must be considered.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the problem explicitly states or implies steady currents. If currents are time-varying, flag the solution for missing displacement current contributions and suggest using Maxwell's equations.
common_errors: Applying Biot-Savart or Ampere's Law to time-varying currents
Ignoring the displacement current term in time-varying cases
Assuming steady current without verifying conditions

rules.title: Verify dimensional and unit consistency in calculations
rules.description: The magnetic field B has units of teslas (T) in the SI system, and its dimensions are [M][T]⁻²[A]⁻¹. Ensure all terms in the Biot-Savart and Ampere's Law equations conform to these units.
rules.check_logic: Check each term in the equations for consistent units. For example, μ₀ has units of T·m/A, and r² should be in meters². Verify that the final magnetic field result has units of teslas.
common_errors: Omitting or miscalculating the μ₀ constant
Using incorrect units for distance (r) or current (I)
Mismatch in units between magnetic field B and other terms

rules.title: Verify magnetic field direction consistency
rules.description: The direction of the magnetic field calculated using Biot-Savart Law or Ampere's Law must conform to the right-hand rule or symmetry arguments.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the calculated field direction follows the right-hand rule for current-carrying wires or symmetry constraints for Ampere's Law. Verify that the direction is consistent with the problem's setup and assumptions.
common_errors: Incorrect use of the right-hand rule for field direction
Ignoring symmetry constraints for field direction in Ampere's Law
Reversing the field direction due to sign convention errors

rules.title: Ensure superposition principle is applied when multiple sources exist
rules.description: The magnetic field due to multiple current elements is the vector sum of the fields produced by each element, as per the superposition principle.
rules.check_logic: Check if the magnetic field contributions from all current elements are added vectorially to find the total field. Ensure no contributions are neglected.
common_errors: Adding magnetic field contributions algebraically instead of vectorially
Neglecting contributions from some current elements
Incorrectly combining fields from different sources

rules.title: Verify boundary conditions at interfaces
rules.description: At the boundary between two media, the tangential component of the magnetic field B and the normal component of the magnetic flux density B·n must satisfy continuity conditions.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the tangential component of B is continuous across the boundary, and the normal component of B·n accounts for any surface currents or discontinuities.
common_errors: Ignoring surface currents at boundaries
Incorrectly applying continuity conditions for B
Neglecting the effect of material properties on B

rules.title: Verify correctness of Faraday's Law in integral form
rules.description: Faraday's Law in integral form states that the line integral of the electric field around a closed loop is equal to the negative rate of change of magnetic flux through the surface bounded by the loop: ∮E·dl = -dΦB/dt. This applies to any closed loop and surface that are geometrically consistent.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the calculated line integral of E (∮E·dl) equals -dΦB/dt, where ΦB = ∫B·dA. Check that the chosen surface matches the loop and that the time variation of B is correctly accounted for.
common_errors: Using the wrong sign for the rate of change of magnetic flux.
Incorrectly calculating the magnetic flux ΦB.
Misalignment between the loop and the chosen surface.

rules.title: Ensure correct application of Lenz's Law for induced EMF
rules.description: Lenz's Law states that the direction of the induced EMF opposes the change in magnetic flux that caused it, reflected in the negative sign in Faraday's Law.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the direction of the induced current (or EMF) is consistent with opposing the change in magnetic flux. Confirm that the calculated direction fits with the problem's coordinate system.
common_errors: Reversing the direction of induced EMF or current.
Ignoring the negative sign in Faraday's Law.
Inconsistent use of coordinate system conventions.

rules.title: Check correctness of magnetic flux calculation
rules.description: Magnetic flux (ΦB) is defined as ΦB = ∫B·dA, where B is the magnetic field and dA is the infinitesimal area vector. Ensure that the integration is correctly performed over the surface of interest.
rules.check_logic: Verify that B and dA are properly aligned, and the dot product is computed correctly. Ensure the integration bounds match the chosen surface.
common_errors: Overlooking the angle between B and dA in the dot product.
Using incorrect integration limits for the surface.
Mixing up scalar and vector forms of magnetic flux.

rules.title: Verify induced EMF in moving conductors using v × B
rules.description: For a conductor moving through a magnetic field, the induced EMF is given by E = v × B, where v is the velocity of the conductor and B is the magnetic field.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the cross product v × B is calculated correctly. Check that the direction of the induced EMF matches the right-hand rule and is consistent with the problem's coordinate system.
common_errors: Incorrectly computing the cross product.
Using the wrong sign or direction for the velocity vector.
Failing to account for all components of the magnetic field.

rules.title: Check dimensional consistency for EMF calculations
rules.description: The induced EMF has the unit of voltage (V), equivalent to joules per coulomb (J/C). Ensure all terms in the equations for EMF result in consistent dimensions.
rules.check_logic: Verify that both sides of the equation for EMF have consistent units. For example, ensure v × B has units of voltage (V) when applied to a conductor of length l in a magnetic field.
common_errors: Mixing up units of velocity, magnetic field, and EMF.
Failing to include the length of the conductor in motion-induced EMF problems.
Incorrectly simplifying unit expressions.

rules.title: Ensure validity conditions for Faraday's Law
rules.description: Faraday's Law is valid only in the absence of relativistic effects and in non-quantum mechanical contexts. It assumes the magnetic and electric fields are well-defined and continuous.
rules.check_logic: Check that the problem does not involve relativistic speeds or quantum mechanical effects. Confirm that the magnetic and electric fields are continuous and well-behaved within the region of interest.
common_errors: Applying Faraday's Law in cases involving relativistic effects.
Ignoring discontinuities in the magnetic or electric fields.

rules.title: Verify consistency of closed loop geometry
rules.description: The loop used in Faraday's Law must be a closed curve. The surface bound by the loop must be well-defined and consistent with the loop geometry.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the chosen loop is closed and that the surface for magnetic flux calculation is properly bounded by the loop.
common_errors: Using an open curve instead of a closed loop.
Mismatch between the loop and the surface geometry.

rules.title: Check time dependence of magnetic flux for induced EMF
rules.description: The induced EMF depends on the time rate of change of magnetic flux (dΦB/dt). Ensure that time dependence is correctly included in problems involving time-varying magnetic fields.
rules.check_logic: Verify that dΦB/dt is calculated accurately by differentiating the magnetic flux concerning time. Ensure the time-dependent quantities (e.g., B(t) or the area A(t)) are properly expressed.
common_errors: Forgetting to differentiate the magnetic flux concerning time.
Omitting time dependence of the magnetic field or area.
Using incorrect expressions for time-varying quantities.

rules.title: Check polarity of induced EMF
rules.description: Lenz's Law states that the direction of the induced EMF opposes the change in magnetic flux that causes it. This ensures conservation of energy and applies universally to electromagnetic induction.
rules.check_logic: Verify if the induced current's direction (or EMF polarity) is such that it creates a magnetic field opposing the change in magnetic flux (e.g., increasing flux induces a current creating a magnetic field in the opposite direction). Use the right-hand rule to confirm the direction of the induced current.
common_errors: Incorrect direction of induced current or EMF.
Forgetting to apply the opposition principle of Lenz's Law.
Confusing the direction of magnetic flux change with the field direction.

rules.title: Verify magnetic flux rate of change in Faraday's Law
rules.description: Faraday's Law of Induction relates the magnitude of the induced EMF to the rate of change of magnetic flux through a loop. The induced EMF is given by E = -dΦ/dt.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the magnetic flux Φ is calculated correctly as the product of the magnetic field, area, and cosine of the angle between them (Φ = B·A·cosθ). Then, compute the time derivative accurately, ensuring the correct sign convention is applied.
common_errors: Miscalculating the magnetic flux (e.g., not considering the angle θ or area).
Incorrect differentiation of flux with respect to time.
Using the wrong sign convention for induced EMF.

rules.title: Check for resistance in eddy current paths
rules.description: Eddy currents are induced in conductive materials when there is a change in magnetic flux. The magnitude of these currents depends on the material's electrical resistance and the rate of flux change.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the material's resistivity, thickness, and geometry are considered when calculating the magnitude of eddy currents (e.g., I ∝ 1/R, where R is resistance). Ensure that the induced currents form closed loops within the material.
common_errors: Neglecting the resistive properties of the material.
Assuming eddy currents form without considering the conductive path geometry.
Ignoring the proportionality to the rate of flux change.

rules.title: Check conservation of energy in induced currents
rules.description: The work done by the induced current must equal the energy associated with the changing magnetic flux. This ensures no energy is created or destroyed, consistent with Lenz's Law.
rules.check_logic: Verify if the power dissipated in resistive losses (P = I²R) matches the rate of energy transfer due to the changing flux (|dΦ/dt|). Ensure that energy conservation is maintained in the system.
common_errors: Ignoring energy conservation when analyzing the system.
Miscalculating resistive power losses.
Neglecting the energy associated with the magnetic flux change.

rules.title: Verify sign convention for flux change
rules.description: The sign of the induced EMF depends on whether the magnetic flux is increasing or decreasing. Positive flux change induces a negative EMF, and negative flux change induces a positive EMF.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the sign of dΦ/dt is correctly determined based on the flux direction and whether it is increasing or decreasing. Confirm that the negative sign in Faraday's Law is applied correctly.
common_errors: Forgetting the negative sign in Faraday's Law.
Misinterpreting the direction of flux change.
Using incorrect signs for induced EMF or current.

rules.title: Confirm applicability for non-static fields
rules.description: Lenz's Law and Faraday's Law apply only when the magnetic field is dynamic (changing with time). Static magnetic fields do not induce currents.
rules.check_logic: Check if the magnetic field is time-varying. If the field is static (dB/dt = 0), no EMF or current should be induced. Ensure that any assumptions about field dynamics are explicitly stated.
common_errors: Applying Lenz's or Faraday's Law to static magnetic fields.
Assuming induced EMF in the absence of flux change.
Forgetting to check the time-dependence of the field.

rules.title: Ensure correct use of coordinate system for flux direction
rules.description: The direction of the magnetic flux and the induced current must be analyzed using a consistent coordinate system. Use the right-hand rule to determine the direction of the induced current.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the right-hand rule is applied correctly, where the thumb points in the direction of the magnetic flux and the curled fingers indicate the induced current direction. Ensure the coordinate system is consistent throughout the analysis.
common_errors: Using the left-hand rule instead of the right-hand rule.
Inconsistent coordinate system for flux and current analysis.
Misinterpreting the relationship between flux direction and current.

rules.title: Check dimensional consistency of induced EMF
rules.description: The induced EMF should have the correct units of volts (V), which are equivalent to Weber per second (Wb/s). This ensures consistency in Faraday's Law calculations.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the units of dΦ/dt are Weber per second (Wb/s) and match the units of EMF (volts). Verify that all intermediate calculations maintain dimensional consistency.
common_errors: Forgetting to use consistent units for flux and time.
Mixing up units of area, magnetic field, or angle when calculating flux.
Failing to verify dimensional consistency in intermediate calculations.

rules.title: Verify mutual inductance in coupled circuits
rules.description: When two circuits are magnetically coupled, a change in current in one circuit induces an EMF in the other. The mutual inductance M quantifies this coupling.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the mutual inductance M is calculated correctly using the formula M = (N2Φ2)/I1, where N2 is the number of turns in the secondary coil, Φ2 is the flux linkage, and I1 is the current in the primary coil. Verify that the induced EMF in the secondary coil is E2 = -M(dI1/dt).
common_errors: Incorrect calculation of mutual inductance.
Neglecting the coupling factor between the circuits.
Forgetting to account for the time rate of change of current in the primary coil.

rules.title: Apply Fundamental Inductance Equations
rules.description: Self-inductance describes the voltage induced in a coil due to a change in current through the same coil. It is given by V = -L*(dI/dt), whereas mutual inductance describes the induced voltage in a coil due to a change in current in another coil, represented by V_2 = -M*(dI_1/dt).
rules.check_logic: Verify if the voltage induced in a coil is calculated using the correct form of the inductance equation: self-inductance for the same coil and mutual inductance for different coils. Ensure the equations are applied to the correct physical context.
common_errors: Using mutual inductance formula for self-inductance problems
Neglecting the negative sign indicating induced emf opposes the change
Confusing the roles of L (self-inductance) and M (mutual inductance)

rules.title: Verify Inductance Sign Convention
rules.description: The negative sign in both self and mutual inductance equations represents Lenz's Law, indicating that the induced emf will oppose the change in current that caused it.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the negative sign is included and correctly applied in all calculations involving induced emf, and verify that the opposition to the change in current is consistent with Lenz's Law.
common_errors: Omitting the negative sign
Incorrect application leading to opposition of current increase
Misinterpreting the physical meaning of the negative sign

rules.title: Check Validity for Inductance Formulas Application
rules.description: Inductance formulas are valid under conditions where the system can be considered linear, magnetic fields can be approximated as uniform on short time scales, and the materials involved do not exhibit hysteresis or saturation effects.
rules.check_logic: Determine if the system's assumptions regarding linearity, uniform magnetic fields, and material properties hold true for the context of the problem.
common_errors: Applied in nonlinear regimes without correction
Assuming uniform fields where large spatial gradients exist
Ignoring material saturation or hysteresis effects

rules.title: Ensure Dimensional Consistency in Induction Calculations
rules.description: The unit of inductance is Henry (H), which corresponds to Volts per Ampere-second. Ensure calculations maintain dimensional consistency with respect to time, current, and induced voltage.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all inductance-related formulas maintain dimensional consistency, and ensure proper unit conversions are applied where necessary.
common_errors: Incorrect unit conversion in voltage calculations
Mistaking inductance units as simple power or energy units
Mixing incompatible units in intermediate steps

rules.title: Assess Geometric Constraints on Inductance
rules.description: Inductance depends on geometric factors such as the number of coil turns, cross-sectional area, and core permeability. These factors must be explicitly considered and consistent with the setup described in the problem.
rules.check_logic: Ensure calculations consider the actual geometry of the coils involved, including the number of turns, cross-sectional area, and the material properties of the core.
common_errors: Neglecting the effect of core permeability
Incorrect counting of coil turns
Assuming ideal geometry without verifying physical constraints

rules.title: Account for Mutual Inductance in Multiple-Coil Systems
rules.description: Mutual inductance between coils depends on their relative positions, orientations, and the magnetic coupling factor between them.
rules.check_logic: Validate the assumptions concerning coil orientation, distance, and coupling factor when calculating mutual inductance. Ensure that misalignments or weak coupling are accounted for.
common_errors: Ignoring mutual interference effects
Assuming mutual inductance is unaffected by coil misalignment
Overestimating coupling factor in loosely coupled systems

rules.title: Ensure Kinematic Consistency in Time-Changed Current
rules.description: Consistency between time rates of change (dI/dt for current change) and induced emf is crucial, particularly when mechanical motion influences magnetic flux change.
rules.check_logic: Check equations to ensure proper correlation between mechanical motion variables (e.g., velocity, displacement) and electromagnetic induction. Verify that dynamic effects, such as frequency dependence, are correctly incorporated.
common_errors: Failing to relate mechanical motion with current change rate
Ignoring dynamic frequency effects
Neglecting induced emf contributions from moving conductors

rules.title: Verify Energy Storage in Inductors
rules.description: Inductors store energy in their magnetic fields, given by the formula U = (1/2)*L*I^2 for self-inductance. Ensure energy storage calculations are consistent with the inductance and current values.
rules.check_logic: Verify that energy storage calculations use the correct inductance and current values, and ensure the formula is applied correctly.
common_errors: Using incorrect inductance or current values
Neglecting energy contributions in coupled systems
Misinterpreting energy storage as power dissipation

rules.title: Verify Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) for RL Circuits
rules.description: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law states that the sum of potential differences (voltage) in a closed loop is zero. For an RL circuit, this means the sum of the voltage across the resistor and the inductor must equal the applied EMF (if present).
rules.check_logic: Verify that V_R + V_L = V_source (if no source is present, ensure V_R + V_L = 0).
common_errors: Forgetting to include the self-induced EMF across the inductor (L di/dt).
Incorrect sign for the voltage across the inductor due to improper orientation.
Treating the inductor as a resistor and using Ohm's Law incorrectly.

rules.title: Verify RC Circuit Time Constant Calculation
rules.description: The time constant of an RC circuit is given by τ = RC. It characterizes the rate at which the capacitor charges or discharges to about 63% of its final voltage value.
rules.check_logic: Check if the time constant is calculated as the product of resistance (R) and capacitance (C), and ensure units are in seconds.
common_errors: Using the reciprocal of RC instead of the product.
Misinterpreting the time constant as the time for full charge/discharge instead of 63%.
Incorrect units for time constant (should be seconds).

rules.title: Verify Resonance Frequency Calculation in RLC Circuits
rules.description: The resonance frequency (f₀) in an RLC circuit is determined by the formula f₀ = 1 / (2π√(LC)), where L is the inductance and C is the capacitance.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the resonance frequency is computed using the correct formula, and verify that the units of L and C are consistent.
common_errors: Forgetting the 2π factor in the denominator.
Using incorrect or mismatched units for L or C (e.g., H vs. mH or F vs. μF).
Confusing angular frequency (ω₀) with resonance frequency (f₀).

rules.title: Ensure Proper Sign Convention for Voltages in Circuits
rules.description: Voltages should follow the passive sign convention: current entering the positive terminal of a passive element corresponds to a voltage drop.
rules.check_logic: Verify that voltage drops across resistors, inductors, and capacitors are consistent with current direction and follow the passive sign convention.
common_errors: Reversing the voltage sign for a resistor or inductor.
Incorrectly assuming the same voltage drop direction for all elements in the circuit.
Neglecting to account for the polarity of the voltage source.

rules.title: Check Energy Conservation in RC and RL Circuits
rules.description: Energy conservation should hold true in RC and RL circuits. Energy is stored in the capacitor for RC circuits and in the inductor for RL circuits. The energy supplied by sources must equal the energy dissipated and stored.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the supplied energy equals the sum of dissipated (I²R) and stored energy (1/2 CV² for capacitors or 1/2 LI² for inductors).
common_errors: Neglecting the energy stored in the capacitor or inductor.
Incorrectly calculating dissipated energy using P = IV instead of P = I²R.
Ignoring the work done by the source.

rules.title: Ensure Dimensional Consistency in RLC Circuit Calculations
rules.description: Each equation in RLC circuit analysis must be dimensionally consistent. For example, the terms in V = IR + L(di/dt) or V = Q/C must all have units of voltage (V).
rules.check_logic: Ensure that all terms in equations have consistent units, particularly for voltage, current, resistance, capacitance, inductance, and charge.
common_errors: Using mismatched units like ohms with millihenries or microfarads without converting.
Forgetting to convert time units when using derivatives (e.g., di/dt).
Failing to ensure that all terms in voltage equations are expressed in volts.

rules.title: Validate Conditions for Phasor Analysis in AC Circuits
rules.description: Phasor analysis is valid only for sinusoidal steady-state AC signals. It cannot be applied to transient or non-sinusoidal waveforms.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the circuit operates in steady-state AC with sinusoidal sources before applying phasor analysis.
common_errors: Applying phasor methods to DC circuits or transient states.
Ignoring the need for sinusoidal sources.
Using incorrect angular frequency (ω) in phasor calculations.

rules.title: Verify Initial and Final Conditions for RC and RL Circuits
rules.description: In RC and RL circuits, the initial and final conditions of the capacitor voltage and inductor current are critical. A capacitor's voltage cannot change instantaneously, and an inductor's current cannot change instantaneously due to energy-storage properties.
rules.check_logic: Check if the initial capacitor voltage and inductor current are used correctly and that changes occur gradually based on the circuit's time constant.
common_errors: Assuming instant changes in capacitor voltage or inductor current.
Neglecting to account for initial conditions when solving differential equations.
Confusing the behavior of capacitors and inductors during switching events.

rules.title: Verify Gauss's Law for Electric Fields
rules.description: Gauss's Law states that the total electric flux through a closed surface equals the total charge enclosed divided by the permittivity of free space (ε_0). This law applies in both static and dynamic scenarios involving electric fields.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the integral of the electric field dot product with the normal surface area vector equals the enclosed charge divided by ε_0.
common_errors: Failing to account for all enclosed charges.
Using incorrect surface normals for the flux calculation.
Omitting the permittivity constant (ε_0).
Misinterpreting open surfaces as closed surfaces.

rules.title: Verify Gauss's Law for Magnetism
rules.description: Gauss's Law for magnetism states that the total magnetic flux through any closed surface is always zero, indicating the non-existence of magnetic monopoles.
rules.check_logic: Check that the integral of the magnetic field dot product with the normal surface area vector equals zero for any closed surface.
common_errors: Assuming non-zero flux for magnetic fields through closed surfaces.
Incorrectly applying this law to open surfaces.
Improperly handling vector directions for normal components.

rules.title: Verify Faraday's Law of Induction
rules.description: Faraday's Law states that the electromotive force (EMF) around a closed loop equals the negative rate of change of the magnetic flux through the loop. This law is relevant for time-varying magnetic fields.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the line integral of the electric field around the loop equals the negative time derivative of the magnetic flux through the loop.
common_errors: Neglecting the negative sign (Lenz's Law).
Mixing up integration limits for the loop.
Forgetting to calculate the rate of change of magnetic flux.
Omitting contributions from time-varying magnetic fields.

rules.title: Verify Ampere-Maxwell's Law
rules.description: Ampere-Maxwell's Law states that the line integral of the magnetic field around a closed loop equals the permeability of free space (μ_0) times the sum of conduction current and displacement current through the loop.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the line integral of the magnetic field equals μ_0 times the sum of conduction current and the time derivative of the electric flux density through the loop.
common_errors: Failing to include displacement current in time-varying cases.
Omitting the permeability constant (μ_0).
Using incorrect integration paths for the loop.
Ignoring contributions from non-uniform current densities.

rules.title: Check Sign Conventions in Maxwell's Equations
rules.description: The signs in Maxwell's equations depend on orientation rules, mainly the right-hand rule for vector cross products. Incorrect sign conventions lead to errors in calculations.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the surface normals, loop directions, and vector cross products adhere to the right-hand rule and match the chosen coordinate system.
common_errors: Using left-hand rule instead of right-hand rule.
Reversing the orientation of surface normals.
Flipping the direction of closed loop integration.

rules.title: Validate Boundary Conditions for Fields
rules.description: At the boundary between two media, tangential components of the electric and magnetic fields must be continuous, while normal components depend on surface charge and surface current densities.
rules.check_logic: Ensure boundary conditions are satisfied for both electric and magnetic fields across the interface between two media.
common_errors: Assuming continuity of normal electric fields when surface charges are present.
Neglecting surface currents when analyzing magnetic field boundaries.
Failing to consider dielectric properties of the media.

rules.title: Check Dimensional and Unit Consistency
rules.description: Each term in Maxwell's equations must exhibit consistent dimensions and units, including flux, fields, charge density, and current density.
rules.check_logic: Ensure all terms in the equations have consistent units (e.g., electric field in V/m, magnetic field in T, charge density in C/m³, etc.).
common_errors: Incorrectly converting between units (e.g., from Gauss to Tesla).
Omitting unit conversions when using derived quantities.
Using incompatible units across terms in the equations.

rules.title: Verify Validity Conditions for Maxwell's Equations
rules.description: Maxwell's equations assume classical conditions like non-relativistic speeds and neglect quantum effects. They also assume continuous media without abrupt discontinuities unless explicitly accounted for.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the problem context is within the classical regime and that media are continuous unless specified otherwise.
common_errors: Applying Maxwell's equations to quantum-scale systems.
Neglecting relativistic corrections at high speeds.
Using Maxwell's equations without considering boundary conditions in discontinuous media.

rules.title: Verify Maxwell's wave equation for electric and magnetic fields
rules.description: The electric field (E) and magnetic field (B) components of an electromagnetic wave must satisfy Maxwell's wave equation in free space: ∇²E = (1/c²)(∂²E/∂t²) and ∇²B = (1/c²)(∂²B/∂t²), where c is the speed of light in vacuum. This applies to harmonic plane waves in free space.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the second spatial derivatives of the fields (E and B) are proportional to the second time derivatives, with the proportionality constant being 1/c². Verify this for harmonic plane waves in free space.
common_errors: Not including the 1/c² factor in the wave equation.
Incorrectly applying the wave equation to non-harmonic fields.
Omitting the time-dependent component in wave analysis.

rules.title: Validate the Poynting vector calculation
rules.description: The Poynting vector (S = E × B/μ₀) represents the energy flux density of an electromagnetic wave. It should be perpendicular to both E and B and point in the direction of wave propagation. This applies to plane electromagnetic waves in free space.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the Poynting vector is calculated as the cross product of E and B. Ensure its direction aligns with the propagation direction and its magnitude corresponds to the energy flux. Confirm the division by μ₀ is correctly applied.
common_errors: Using incorrect cross-product order (e.g., B × E instead of E × B).
Forgetting the division by μ₀ for the Poynting vector magnitude.
Misidentifying the direction of wave propagation.

rules.title: Check orthogonality of E, B, and wave propagation direction
rules.description: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric field (E), magnetic field (B), and wave propagation direction (k) must be mutually perpendicular. This holds true for plane waves in homogeneous, isotropic media.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the dot products E · B, E · k, and B · k are all zero. Confirm that the cross-product relationships between E, B, and k are consistent with the right-hand rule.
common_errors: Assuming E and B are parallel instead of perpendicular.
Incorrectly identifying the propagation direction.
Failing to verify orthogonality conditions.

rules.title: Validate the speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum
rules.description: The speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum is given by c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀), where ε₀ is the permittivity and μ₀ is the permeability of free space. This is a fundamental constant of nature.
rules.check_logic: Verify the calculated wave speed matches c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s within reasonable tolerances. Ensure the correct values for ε₀ and μ₀ are used.
common_errors: Using incorrect values for ε₀ or μ₀.
Assuming the wave speed differs in a vacuum.
Failing to account for medium properties if not in a vacuum.

rules.title: Verify energy density expressions
rules.description: The total energy density of an electromagnetic wave is the sum of the electric field energy density (u_E = 1/2 ε₀ E²) and the magnetic field energy density (u_B = 1/2 B²/μ₀). This applies to monochromatic plane waves in free space.
rules.check_logic: Check that the total energy density u = u_E + u_B is used and that u_E and u_B are correctly calculated from E and B. Confirm that the energy densities are consistent with the wave's properties.
common_errors: Forgetting to square the E or B field in the energy density expressions.
Neglecting the 1/2 factor in the energy density formulas.
Incorrectly equating u_E and u_B without justification.

rules.title: Ensure dimensional consistency in wave equations
rules.description: All terms in the wave equations, energy density formulas, and Poynting vector must have consistent dimensions. For example, the Poynting vector has dimensions of power per unit area (W/m²), and energy densities have dimensions of energy per unit volume (J/m³).
rules.check_logic: Verify units in all equations and results. For instance, check that the Poynting vector has dimensions of W/m² and energy densities are in J/m³. Ensure that derived quantities match their expected physical dimensions.
common_errors: Mixing up the units of E and B fields.
Failing to convert units of energy density or flux correctly.
Not checking that all terms in equations have consistent dimensions.

rules.title: Check boundary conditions for electromagnetic waves
rules.description: At the interface between two media, the tangential components of E and H (H = B/μ) must be continuous, and the normal components of D (D = εE) and B must also satisfy boundary conditions based on the properties of the media.
rules.check_logic: Ensure appropriate continuity conditions are applied at boundaries. Verify calculations for transmitted and reflected waves, ensuring they satisfy Snell's law and Fresnel equations where applicable.
common_errors: Forgetting to apply boundary conditions at interfaces.
Incorrectly matching tangential or normal components.
Neglecting the material properties (ε, μ) in boundary conditions.

rules.title: Validate polarization state of the wave
rules.description: An electromagnetic wave can be linearly, circularly, or elliptically polarized, depending on the relative phase and amplitudes of the electric field components. The polarization direction is orthogonal to the propagation direction.
rules.check_logic: Verify the relative phase and amplitude of electric field components to determine the polarization state. Ensure polarization direction is orthogonal to the wave vector. Confirm the phase difference is consistent with the stated polarization type.
common_errors: Confusing linear polarization with circular or elliptical.
Incorrectly identifying the polarization direction.
Neglecting the phase difference between field components.

rules.title: Verify wave impedance in free space
rules.description: The wave impedance in free space is given by Z₀ = √(μ₀/ε₀), which relates the magnitudes of the electric and magnetic fields in an electromagnetic wave.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the ratio of E to B in free space matches Z₀ ≈ 377 Ω. Verify calculations involving wave impedance are consistent with this value.
common_errors: Using incorrect values for μ₀ or ε₀.
Failing to verify the E/B ratio matches the wave impedance.
Confusing wave impedance with characteristic impedance of a medium.

rules.title: Verify the definition of the Poynting vector
rules.description: The Poynting vector is defined as S = (1/μ₀) (E × B), where E is the electric field, B is the magnetic field, and μ₀ is the permeability of free space. It represents the energy flux density of an electromagnetic wave.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the Poynting vector S is computed using the cross product of E and B, scaled by 1/μ₀, and that the direction is consistent with the right-hand rule.
common_errors: Using a dot product instead of a cross product between E and B.
Missing the scaling factor 1/μ₀.
Incorrectly computing the direction of S due to improper application of the right-hand rule.

rules.title: Check the formula for radiation pressure
rules.description: Radiation pressure is given by P = S/c for perfectly absorbing surfaces and P = 2S/c for perfectly reflecting surfaces, where S is the magnitude of the Poynting vector and c is the speed of light in a vacuum.
rules.check_logic: Check if the formula for radiation pressure correctly uses S/c or 2S/c depending on the nature of the surface (absorbing or reflecting), and ensure that the speed of light c is correctly substituted.
common_errors: Using the wrong factor (e.g., using 2S/c instead of S/c for an absorbing surface).
Forgetting to divide S by c.
Incorrect substitution of the speed of light c.

rules.title: Verify energy conservation in electromagnetic waves
rules.description: The energy density of an electromagnetic wave is split equally between the electric and magnetic fields, with total energy density given by u = (ε₀E² + B²/μ₀)/2. The Poynting vector should represent the flow of this energy.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the total energy density u is correctly computed, the contributions from both electric and magnetic fields are included, and the Poynting vector aligns with the energy flow direction.
common_errors: Incorrect computation of energy density (e.g., forgetting the factor of 1/2).
Ignoring the contribution from either the electric or magnetic field.
Misalignment between the direction of S and the wave propagation direction.

rules.title: Check dimensional consistency of Poynting vector and radiation pressure
rules.description: The Poynting vector must have units of energy flux density (W/m²), and radiation pressure must have units of force per unit area (N/m²).
rules.check_logic: Verify that the units of S are W/m² and the units of P are N/m² in the final expressions, and ensure proper unit conversions if non-SI units are used.
common_errors: Mixing up units of electric and magnetic fields in calculations.
Forgetting to include μ₀ or c, leading to incorrect units for S or P.
Incorrect unit conversions when working in non-SI units.

rules.title: Verify the direction of the Poynting vector
rules.description: The direction of the Poynting vector is given by the right-hand rule applied to E × B. It must point in the direction of energy propagation in the electromagnetic wave.
rules.check_logic: Check that the cross product of E and B is computed correctly, the right-hand rule is applied, and the resulting vector points in the expected direction of wave propagation.
common_errors: Using the left-hand rule instead of the right-hand rule.
Incorrectly determining the orientation of E or B.
Misinterpreting the direction of the wave propagation.

rules.title: Check boundary conditions for E, B, and S at interfaces
rules.description: At the boundary between two media, the normal component of B and the tangential component of E must be continuous (assuming no surface currents or charges). The Poynting vector must adjust to match the energy flow across the interface.
rules.check_logic: Verify that boundary conditions are applied correctly to E and B, and ensure that the Poynting vector is consistent with these conditions, accounting for reflection and refraction effects.
common_errors: Ignoring continuity conditions for E and B at boundaries.
Incorrectly computing the Poynting vector in the second medium.
Forgetting to account for reflection or refraction effects at the interface.

rules.title: Verify validity conditions for applying the Poynting vector
rules.description: The Poynting vector formulation assumes linear, isotropic, and non-dispersive media. It may not be accurate in plasmas, anisotropic materials, or dispersive media.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the problem specifies conditions (e.g., linear and isotropic media) under which the Poynting vector can be applied, and verify that corrections are made for non-linear or dispersive media if necessary.
common_errors: Applying the Poynting vector in dispersive or anisotropic media without appropriate corrections.
Ignoring material properties that affect E and B relationships.
Using the Poynting vector in scenarios involving significant material non-linearities.

rules.title: Ensure consistency in coordinate system usage
rules.description: The electric field (E), magnetic field (B), and Poynting vector (S) must all be defined in a consistent coordinate system, with directions clearly stated and aligned.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that all vector components are expressed in the same coordinate system and that transformations, if any, are correctly applied.
common_errors: Mixing Cartesian and spherical coordinates without proper transformation.
Defining E and B in different coordinate systems without converting one to match the other.
Neglecting clear specification of the coordinate system in the problem setup.

rules.title: Verify time-averaged Poynting vector for sinusoidal waves
rules.description: For sinusoidal electromagnetic waves, the time-averaged Poynting vector is given by ⟨S⟩ = (1/2μ₀) Re(E₀ × B₀*), where E₀ and B₀ are the complex amplitudes of the electric and magnetic fields, and * denotes the complex conjugate.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the time-averaged Poynting vector is computed correctly using the complex amplitudes of E and B, and verify that the factor of 1/2 is included.
common_errors: Forgetting the factor of 1/2 for time-averaged quantities.
Incorrectly handling the complex conjugate of B₀.
Using instantaneous fields instead of complex amplitudes.

rules.title: Verify Dipole Moment Calculation
rules.description: Check the calculation of the electric dipole moment, defined as the product of charge separation distance and charge magnitude for two opposite charges.
rules.check_logic: Ensure dipole moment p = q * d, where q is the charge and d is the separation vector between charges. Verify that the direction of d points from the negative charge to the positive charge.
common_errors: Confusing dipole moment with electrical force
Incorrect vector direction for d
Incorrect charge magnitude used

rules.title: Validate Electric Field from Dipole
rules.description: Ensure that the electric field due to a dipole is calculated using the correct formula for a field point and considering the dipole axis.
rules.check_logic: Verify E = (1/(4πϵ₀)) * (p/r³) * (2cosθ * r̂ + sinθ * θ̂), where p is the dipole moment, r is the distance from the dipole, and θ is the angle with the dipole axis. Confirm that the unit vectors r̂ and θ̂ are correctly defined in spherical coordinates.
common_errors: Ignoring angle θ in field calculation
Incorrect unit vectors usage
Using r² instead of r³

rules.title: Check Conditions for Multipole Expansion
rules.description: Multipole expansion is valid when the distance to the field point is much larger than the typical length of the charge distribution.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that r >> d, where r is the distance to the field point and d is the size of the dipole. Verify that higher-order terms are included if r is not sufficiently large.
common_errors: Applying multipole expansion for r ~ d
Ignoring higher-order terms when r is not sufficiently large

rules.title: Verify Spherical Coordinate System
rules.description: Ensure proper sign conventions and angles are used in spherical coordinates when calculating electric fields and potentials.
rules.check_logic: Check that θ is measured from the positive z-axis and ϕ from the positive x-axis in the xy-plane. Confirm that the coordinate system is right-handed.
common_errors: Using incorrect reference axes for θ and ϕ
Misinterpreting the angle conventions leading to incorrect field vectors
Using a left-handed coordinate system instead of right-handed

rules.title: Check Potential Energy of Dipole in Electric Field
rules.description: Ensure the calculation of potential energy of an electric dipole in a uniform electric field is correct based on U = -p · E.
rules.check_logic: Verify U = -p * E * cosθ, where p is the dipole moment, E is the uniform electric field strength, and θ is the angle between p and E. Confirm that the negative sign is correctly applied to indicate energy minimization.
common_errors: Using plus sign instead of minus in calculation
Incorrect angle used for calculation
Ignoring vector nature leading to scalar multiplication errors

rules.title: Check Dimensional Consistency in Dipole Calculations
rules.description: Ensure that dimensions related to electric dipole and its effects are consistent with electromagnetic principles.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all quantities have correct dimensions, e.g., dipole moment in Cm, electric field in N/C, potential energy in J. Confirm that unit conversions are correctly applied when necessary.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for dipole moment
Misaligning units for energy and field interactions
Neglecting conversion between units when necessary

rules.title: Evaluate Small Angle Approximation
rules.description: Check if small angle approximation is used correctly in the context of dipole interaction particularly for close to polar angles.
rules.check_logic: Ensure sinθ ≈ θ and cosθ ≈ 1 for small θ in calculations involving dipole fields. Verify that the approximation is not applied for large angles.
common_errors: Using approximation incorrectly for large angles
Assuming approximation without verifying angle size
Ignoring terms that contribute when approximation limits are exceeded

rules.title: Verify Torque on Dipole in Electric Field
rules.description: Ensure the calculation of torque on an electric dipole in a uniform electric field is correct.
rules.check_logic: Verify τ = p × E, where τ is the torque, p is the dipole moment, and E is the electric field. Confirm that the direction of torque follows the right-hand rule.
common_errors: Incorrect cross product calculation
Ignoring vector nature of torque
Using incorrect angle between p and E

rules.title: Check Energy Stability of Dipole in Electric Field
rules.description: Ensure the stability of the dipole's orientation in an electric field is correctly analyzed based on potential energy.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the dipole aligns with the electric field to minimize potential energy (U = -p · E). Confirm that misalignment leads to restoring torque.
common_errors: Misinterpreting stable and unstable equilibrium
Ignoring restoring torque for misaligned dipoles
Incorrectly analyzing energy minimization

rules.title: Verify magnetic dipole moment calculation
rules.description: The magnetic dipole moment of a current loop is given by the equation μ = I × A, where I is the current and A is the area vector (A = area × normal unit vector). Ensure the direction of the dipole moment follows the right-hand rule.
rules.check_logic: Check if μ = I × A is used, ensuring current magnitude and area are consistent with their respective units (Amperes, square meters). Verify that the direction of μ is perpendicular to the plane of the loop and follows the right-hand rule.
common_errors: Using incorrect magnitude for current or area
Not applying the right-hand rule for the direction of μ
Forgetting to include the normal vector direction in the area calculation

rules.title: Check magnetic field from a dipole formula
rules.description: The magnetic field due to a dipole at a point in space is derived from B = (μ₀ / 4π) × [(3(μ·r̂)r̂ - μ) / r³], where μ is the magnetic dipole moment, r̂ is the unit vector pointing from the dipole to the observation point, and r is the distance. This applies only for r >> dipole size.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the formula for B is used correctly, with proper vector operations, and ensure r is much larger than the size of the dipole. Confirm that the unit vector r̂ is correctly normalized.
common_errors: Forgetting the r³ factor in the denominator
Incorrectly calculating dot and cross products between vectors
Using the formula for distances comparable to the dipole size
Not normalizing the unit vector r̂

rules.title: Validate sign conventions for coordinate systems
rules.description: The direction of the magnetic dipole moment μ and magnetic field B is determined by standard sign conventions, typically using the right-hand rule for current loops or coordinate systems like Cartesian or spherical coordinates.
rules.check_logic: Check that all directions of vectors (μ, B) are consistent with the right-hand rule. Ensure the chosen coordinate system (Cartesian, spherical, or cylindrical) is explicitly stated and consistently applied throughout the problem.
common_errors: Using left-hand rule instead of the right-hand rule
Mixing Cartesian and spherical coordinate systems without proper transformation
Incorrectly defining unit vectors in spherical or cylindrical systems

rules.title: Ensure boundary conditions for magnetic materials
rules.description: At the boundary between two magnetic materials, the tangential components of H (magnetic field intensity) are continuous, and the normal components of B (magnetic flux density) follow the relation B₁n/μ₁ = B₂n/μ₂.
rules.check_logic: Verify continuity conditions for the tangential component of H and the normal component of B. Ensure proper use of material permeabilities and confirm that the boundary is clearly defined.
common_errors: Neglecting the continuity of H's tangential components
Not accounting for the ratio of B₁n and B₂n based on material permeability
Confusing the roles of H and B in the boundary conditions

rules.title: Validate energy stored in a magnetic dipole in an external field
rules.description: The potential energy of a magnetic dipole μ in an external magnetic field B is given by U = -μ·B. This is a scalar product, and the energy depends on the relative orientation of μ and B.
rules.check_logic: Verify that U = -μ·B is used, with the correct scalar product and orientation between μ and B. Ensure the angle between μ and B is correctly calculated.
common_errors: Forgetting the negative sign in U = -μ·B
Using vector multiplication instead of scalar multiplication
Incorrectly calculating the angle between μ and B

rules.title: Verify hysteresis loop characteristics
rules.description: The hysteresis loop of a magnetic material shows the relationship between B and H during magnetization and demagnetization. Key values like coercivity, retentivity, and saturation magnetization should be correctly identified.
rules.check_logic: Check if the hysteresis loop is correctly plotted and interpreted. Ensure values for coercivity, retentivity, and saturation are appropriately labeled and measured. Confirm that the loop shape matches the expected behavior for the material type.
common_errors: Mislabeling or misinterpreting coercivity and retentivity
Incorrectly plotting the hysteresis loop
Neglecting the saturation magnetization value
Failing to account for material-specific loop characteristics

rules.title: Ensure dimensional consistency in magnetic equations
rules.description: Ensure that all equations used in magnetic dipole and magnetic material problems are dimensionally consistent. For example, μ (Am²), B (T), H (A/m), and energy (J) must align with their respective units.
rules.check_logic: Verify the dimensional consistency of all terms in the equations used, ensuring units are correctly converted and consistent. Check for adherence to the SI unit system unless otherwise specified.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for μ, B, H, or energy
Mixing up unit systems (e.g., SI and CGS)
Neglecting unit conversions for area or distance in calculations

rules.title: Check validity conditions for magnetic dipole approximation
rules.description: The magnetic dipole approximation assumes the observation point is far from the dipole compared to the size of the dipole. This condition is essential for the formulas to hold.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the distance r from the dipole to the observation point satisfies r >> size of the dipole. Confirm that the dipole size is explicitly stated or estimated.
common_errors: Applying the dipole approximation to points too close to the dipole
Ignoring the spatial extent of the dipole in the approximation
Using dipole formulas without verifying the far-field condition

rules.title: Verify nonlinearity in magnetic materials
rules.description: Magnetic materials often exhibit nonlinear behavior, where B is not proportional to H. This is especially true near saturation or in ferromagnetic materials.
rules.check_logic: Check if the nonlinearity of the B-H curve is accounted for, particularly near saturation. Ensure that any approximations assume linearity only in the appropriate range.
common_errors: Assuming linearity in the B-H relationship near saturation
Neglecting hysteresis effects in ferromagnetic materials
Using linear approximations without specifying the valid range

topics.name: Displacement Current and Its Role in Maxwell's Equations

rules.title: Verify Ampère-Maxwell Law Incorporates Displacement Current
