rules.description: The Ampère-Maxwell Law modifies Ampère's Law by including the displacement current term (ε₀ ∂E/∂t). This ensures continuity of the magnetic field in time-varying electric fields.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the displacement current term (ε₀ ∂E/∂t) is correctly added to the conduction current (∇ × B = μ₀(J + ε₀ ∂E/∂t)) in the presence of a time-varying electric field.
common_errors: Omitting the displacement current term in time-varying fields.
Using the wrong sign for the displacement current term.
Confusion between conduction current (J) and displacement current (ε₀ ∂E/∂t).

rules.title: Ensure Correct Sign Convention for Displacement Current
rules.description: The displacement current term (ε₀ ∂E/∂t) must have the correct sign relative to the direction of ∂E/∂t in the coordinate system used.
rules.check_logic: Verify that ε₀ ∂E/∂t is included with the appropriate sign based on the chosen coordinate system and Maxwell's equations. Ensure consistency with the right-hand rule for curl operations.
common_errors: Using inconsistent signs for displacement current in the curl equation.
Incorrectly applying coordinate system conventions (e.g., left-hand vs. right-hand rule).

rules.title: Verify Continuity Equation for Charge Conservation
rules.description: The displacement current ensures consistency with the continuity equation (∇·J = -∂ρ/∂t). This is crucial for charge conservation in scenarios with time-varying electric fields.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the displacement current term balances the continuity equation for a varying charge density (∇·J + ∂ρ/∂t = 0). Ensure that the inclusion of ε₀ ∂E/∂t maintains charge conservation.
common_errors: Ignoring the role of displacement current in maintaining charge conservation.
Misinterpreting the relationship between ∂ρ/∂t and ∇·J.

rules.title: Check Dimensional Consistency of Displacement Current Term
rules.description: The displacement current term ε₀ ∂E/∂t must have the same units as the conduction current density J (Amps per square meter).
rules.check_logic: Verify that ε₀ ∂E/∂t has the correct dimensions (A/m²). Confirm that ε₀ has units of F/m, and ∂E/∂t has units of V/m·s.
common_errors: Wrong units for ε₀ or ∂E/∂t.
Inconsistent units between conduction and displacement currents.

rules.title: Verify Boundary Conditions for Displacement Current
rules.description: At the boundary between two materials, the normal component of the displacement current must be continuous if there are no free surface charges or currents.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the boundary conditions for ε₀ ∂E/∂t are applied correctly, ensuring continuity of the normal component across interfaces. Account for any discontinuities in ε₀ or ∂E/∂t due to material properties.
common_errors: Ignoring boundary conditions for displacement current at material interfaces.
Incorrect treatment of discontinuities in ε₀ or ∂E/∂t.

rules.title: Check Validity Conditions for Maxwell's Equations
rules.description: Maxwell's equations, including the displacement current, are valid in classical electrodynamics. They assume continuous fields and neglect quantum effects.
rules.check_logic: Verify that Maxwell's equations are being applied only in conditions where classical electrodynamics is valid (e.g., no quantum or relativistic effects). Ensure that the fields are continuous and differentiable.
common_errors: Applying Maxwell's equations in quantum or microscopic domains without appropriate modifications.
Assuming fields are continuous in scenarios where they are not.

rules.title: Ensure Consistency Between Faraday's Law and Displacement Current
rules.description: Faraday's Law implies that a time-varying magnetic field induces a curl in the electric field (∇ × E = -∂B/∂t). Displacement current must not violate this relationship.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the introduction of the displacement current term does not lead to inconsistencies with Faraday's Law. Ensure that ∂B/∂t and ∂E/∂t are coupled correctly in Maxwell's equations.
common_errors: Ignoring the coupling between ∂B/∂t and ∂E/∂t in Maxwell's equations.
Introducing mathematical inconsistencies between Faraday's Law and the Ampère-Maxwell Law.

rules.title: Verify Geometric Constraints on Displacement Current
rules.description: The displacement current is significant only in regions where the electric field changes with time. In regions with static fields, it must be zero.
rules.check_logic: Verify that ε₀ ∂E/∂t is correctly set to zero in regions of static electric fields or where ∂E/∂t = 0. Ensure that the displacement current is only included in time-varying scenarios.
common_errors: Including displacement current in regions with static fields.
Failing to identify regions where ∂E/∂t = 0.

rules.title: Verify Contribution of Displacement Current to Energy Density
rules.description: The displacement current contributes to the electromagnetic energy density through the electric field. This must be consistent with the Poynting vector and energy conservation.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the displacement current term is correctly accounted for in the electromagnetic energy density (u = 1/2 ε₀E² + 1/2 μ₀B²) and the Poynting vector (S = E × H).
common_errors: Ignoring the contribution of the displacement current to energy density.
Inconsistent treatment of energy conservation involving displacement current.

rules.title: Apply Gauss's Law to conductors
rules.description: Gauss's Law states that the electric flux through a closed surface is proportional to the enclosed charge. For conductors in electrostatics, the electric field inside the conductor is zero, and all excess charges reside on the surface.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the electric field inside a conductor is set to zero and that surface charge density calculations are consistent with the total charge on the conductor. Ensure that the Gaussian surface is chosen appropriately to exploit symmetry.
common_errors: Incorrectly assuming a nonzero electric field inside a conductor
Forgetting that charges in conductors reside only on the surface
Misapplying Gauss’s Law to regions inside the conductor
Choosing an inappropriate Gaussian surface for the problem

rules.title: Analyze charge distribution in insulators
rules.description: In insulators, charges are fixed and do not move freely. The electric field inside and outside the insulator depends on the specific charge distribution (volume, surface, or line).
rules.check_logic: Check if the electric field is calculated using the correct charge density (e.g., volume density for bulk insulators) and the correct integration method for irregular distributions. Ensure that the charge distribution is consistent with the problem's symmetry.
common_errors: Assuming charges in insulators behave like those in conductors
Using incorrect charge density (e.g., using surface density for a volume distribution)
Neglecting the role of symmetry in simplifying field calculations
Failing to account for non-uniform charge distributions in calculations

rules.title: Apply boundary conditions for electric fields
rules.description: At the boundary between two materials, the perpendicular component of the electric field changes proportional to the surface charge density, while the parallel component remains continuous.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the boundary conditions are applied correctly: the normal electric field accounts for surface charge density, and tangential components match on both sides. Ensure that the permittivity of the materials is considered when calculating field discontinuities.
common_errors: Forgetting that the tangential component of the electric field is continuous
Ignoring the surface charge contribution to the normal electric field
Misinterpreting the orientation of the electric field vectors at the boundary
Failing to account for differences in permittivity between materials

rules.title: Verify constant potential inside a conductor
rules.description: In electrostatics, the electric potential is constant throughout the volume of a conductor and on its surface because the electric field inside is zero.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the potential inside the conductor does not vary and matches the value on the conductor's surface. Verify that the potential is continuous across the boundary of the conductor.
common_errors: Incorrectly assuming a varying potential inside the conductor
Forgetting to match the surface potential with the internal potential
Not accounting for boundary conditions when calculating potential
Assuming discontinuities in potential at the conductor's surface

rules.title: Use correct sign conventions for electric fields and potentials
rules.description: Electric fields point away from positive charges and toward negative charges. Electric potential decreases in the direction of the electric field.
rules.check_logic: Verify that electric field vectors are drawn with the correct direction and that potential differences respect the orientation of the field. Ensure that the relationship between electric field and potential gradient is correctly applied.
common_errors: Reversing the direction of the electric field for a given charge
Assigning incorrect signs to potential differences
Misinterpreting the relationship between electric field and potential gradient
Failing to account for the reference point when calculating potential

rules.title: Check dimensional and unit consistency
rules.description: Ensure that all quantities used in calculations (electric field, potential, charge density, permittivity) have consistent units and dimensions.
rules.check_logic: Verify that formulas have consistent dimensions (e.g., electric field E = V/m, potential V in volts, charge density in C/m^2 or C/m^3). Ensure that unit conversions are correctly applied when necessary.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for charge density or electric field
Mixing SI units with non-SI units (e.g., Gaussian units)
Forgetting to convert permittivity to correct units when using ε_0
Failing to check unit consistency in intermediate steps of calculations

rules.title: Apply the superposition principle correctly
rules.description: The net electric field or potential at a point is the vector sum of contributions from all charges. This principle applies to both conductors and insulators.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the electric field or potential is calculated as the sum of contributions from all individual charges, considering their signs, magnitudes, and distances. Verify that vector addition is performed correctly.
common_errors: Forgetting to include all charge contributions in the summation
Incorrectly adding vector components without proper direction
Neglecting the role of symmetry in simplifying calculations
Failing to account for the relative positions of charges when summing contributions

rules.title: Check electric field uniformity near conductor surfaces
rules.description: For a large, flat conductor, the electric field near the surface is uniform and proportional to the surface charge density. This approximation holds far from edges.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the electric field near a large conductor is calculated as E = σ/ε_0 and that deviations occur only near edges or irregular shapes. Ensure that the approximation is not applied to curved or small surfaces.
common_errors: Assuming uniform fields near edges of a conductor
Using incorrect formulas for surface charge density
Misapplying the uniform field approximation to non-flat surfaces
Failing to account for edge effects in field calculations

rules.title: Verify electric field inside a hollow conductor
rules.description: The electric field inside the cavity of a hollow conductor is zero if no charges are present inside the cavity. This is a direct consequence of Gauss's Law.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the electric field inside the cavity of a hollow conductor is set to zero when no charges are present. Verify that any charges inside the cavity are correctly accounted for in field calculations.
common_errors: Incorrectly assuming a nonzero electric field inside an empty cavity
Failing to account for charges placed inside the cavity
Misapplying Gauss's Law to regions inside the cavity

rules.title: Verify transitivity of thermal equilibrium
rules.description: The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics states that if two systems (A and B) are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system (C), then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This principle underlies the concept of temperature as a measurable quantity.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that if T_A = T_C and T_B = T_C, then T_A = T_B for all systems being compared. Explicitly verify the equality of temperatures for all pairs.
common_errors: Failing to check the transitive relationship between three systems.
Assuming thermal equilibrium without explicitly stating it for all pairs.

rules.title: Check correctness of temperature scale conversions
rules.description: Temperature scales (e.g., Celsius, Kelvin, Fahrenheit) follow specific conversion formulas. Kelvin is the absolute scale and starts from absolute zero. For example, T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15 and T(°F) = (9/5)T(°C) + 32.
rules.check_logic: Validate that the correct conversion formula is applied for the given temperature scales. Ensure intermediate steps are shown for clarity.
common_errors: Incorrect addition/subtraction for Kelvin and Celsius conversion.
Forgetting to multiply by (9/5) or add 32 for Fahrenheit conversion.
Mixing up units (e.g., treating Kelvin as Celsius).

rules.title: Ensure dimensional and unit consistency for temperature
rules.description: Temperature must be expressed in consistent units when used in equations or comparisons. For example, Kelvin should be used in thermodynamic equations involving absolute temperatures.
rules.check_logic: Verify that temperature units are consistent throughout the solution, particularly in equations like PV = nRT or when calculating efficiency. Ensure conversions are performed where necessary.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin in thermodynamic equations.
Treating different temperature units as directly comparable without conversion.
Mixing Kelvin and Rankine scales without conversion.

rules.title: Verify validity conditions for applying the Zeroth Law
rules.description: The Zeroth Law applies only to systems that can exchange heat and are isolated from external influences. Ensure no external work or heat source disrupts equilibrium.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that systems are thermally isolated from external heat sources and that no additional work is being done on the systems. Verify that heat exchange is possible between the systems.
common_errors: Ignoring external heat sources or work being done on the system.
Applying the Zeroth Law to systems not capable of heat exchange.

rules.title: Ensure proper thermometer calibration
rules.description: Thermometers must be calibrated to a known temperature scale (e.g., freezing and boiling points of water at 1 atm) to ensure accurate measurement. Calibration errors invalidate temperature readings.
rules.check_logic: Check if the thermometer is calibrated correctly based on the problem's given temperature scale (Celsius, Kelvin, etc.). Verify reference points like freezing and boiling points, and account for atmospheric pressure if relevant.
common_errors: Using uncalibrated thermometers in calculations.
Assuming perfect calibration without verification of reference points.
Forgetting to account for atmospheric pressure when using boiling/freezing points.

rules.title: Define and identify thermal equilibrium correctly
rules.description: Thermal equilibrium occurs when two or more systems in thermal contact have no net heat flow between them, meaning their temperatures are equal.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the system's temperature equality is explicitly stated when claiming thermal equilibrium. Verify that no net heat flow occurs between the systems.
common_errors: Claiming thermal equilibrium without verifying equal temperatures.
Confusing thermal equilibrium with mechanical or chemical equilibrium.

rules.title: Ensure Zeroth Law is applied only to macroscopic systems
rules.description: The Zeroth Law is a macroscopic principle and does not apply to quantum or microscopic systems where temperature may not be well-defined.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the systems being analyzed are macroscopic and can be described by a well-defined temperature. Ensure the systems are in equilibrium states.
common_errors: Attempting to apply the Zeroth Law to microscopic or quantum systems.
Assuming temperature is meaningful for non-equilibrium states.

rules.title: Ensure temperature is defined as a state variable
rules.description: Temperature is a state variable that depends only on the state of the system and not on the path taken to reach that state. Ensure the solution treats temperature as a property of equilibrium states.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that temperature is treated as a uniform and state-dependent property in the solution. Verify that it is not influenced by the process path.
common_errors: Treating temperature as path-dependent.
Failing to recognize temperature as uniform in equilibrium conditions.

rules.title: Account for uncertainty in temperature measurements
rules.description: Temperature measurements are subject to uncertainties due to instrument precision, calibration, and environmental factors. These uncertainties must be considered in calculations and conclusions.
rules.check_logic: Verify that uncertainties in temperature measurements are accounted for, especially when they impact significant figures or derived quantities.
common_errors: Ignoring measurement uncertainties in calculations.
Overstating the precision of temperature readings.
Failing to propagate uncertainties in derived quantities.

rules.title: Ensure First Law Equation Utilized
rules.description: The First Law of Thermodynamics states that the change in internal energy (ΔU) of a system is equal to the heat added to the system (Q) minus the work done by the system (W), expressed as ΔU = Q - W.
rules.check_logic: Verify if ΔU = Q - W is used and all variables are defined with correct signs. Ensure the equation is applied consistently across the problem.
common_errors: Using incorrect formula variants like ΔU = W - Q
Confusing heat added with heat removed

rules.title: Check Direction of Work and Heat
rules.description: In the First Law of Thermodynamics, heat (Q) added to the system is positive, and work (W) done by the system is positive.
rules.check_logic: Ensure Q and W have correct signs based on their direction with respect to the system. Verify that heat removed from the system is negative and work done on the system is negative.
common_errors: Inverting signs for heat and work
Confusing work done by the system with work done on the system

rules.title: Verify Dimensional Consistency
rules.description: The units for heat (Q), work (W), and change in internal energy (ΔU) must be consistent, typically in Joules (J) in SI units.
rules.check_logic: Ensure all terms in ΔU = Q - W are expressed in compatible units (e.g., Joules). If other units like calories are used, verify proper conversion.
common_errors: Using different units for heat and work
Mixing energy units like Joules and calories without conversion

rules.title: Apply Law to Correct System Type
rules.description: The First Law of Thermodynamics is applicable to closed systems without mass exchange across the boundaries.
rules.check_logic: Check if the system described is closed and fulfills the criteria for applying the First Law. Ensure no mass flow occurs across the system boundary.
common_errors: Applying First Law to open systems
Ignoring boundary conditions related to mass flow

rules.title: Constrain Equation for Isothermal Process
rules.description: In an isothermal process for ideal gases, the change in internal energy (ΔU) is zero, so Q = W.
rules.check_logic: Verify if ΔU = 0 is correctly applied and Q = W condition is met for ideal gas isothermal processes. Ensure the gas is ideal and the process is truly isothermal.
common_errors: Misapplying isothermal condition to non-ideal gases
Forgetting ΔU = 0 for isothermal processes

rules.title: Adiabatic Process Application
rules.description: For adiabatic processes, no heat is exchanged (Q=0), and the First Law simplifies to ΔU = -W.
rules.check_logic: Ensure Q=0 is correctly applied in adiabatic calculations and ΔU = -W is used. Verify that the process is truly adiabatic (no heat exchange).
common_errors: Incorrectly setting Q≠0 for adiabatic cases
Misunderstanding work direction for adiabatic processes

rules.title: Verify Closed Cycle Conditions
rules.description: In a closed thermodynamic cycle, the net change in internal energy is zero, so Σ(Q - W) = 0.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that calculations for cycles result in ΣΔU = 0, checking each step in the cycle. Verify that the system returns to its initial state.
common_errors: Failing to sum cycle stages correctly
Ignoring net zero change in internal energy for cycles

rules.title: Differentiate Types of Work
rules.description: Recognize different types of work (e.g., PV work) and ensure appropriate application in the First Law.
rules.check_logic: Distinguish between work types (PV work versus other forms) and apply correctly in ΔU = Q - W. Verify that the correct work expression is used for the given process.
common_errors: Confusing PV work with electrical work
Ignoring the specificity of work types in energy calculations

rules.title: Verify Heat Transfer Mode
rules.description: Ensure the mode of heat transfer (conduction, convection, or radiation) is consistent with the problem's context.
rules.check_logic: Check if the heat transfer mode is correctly identified and applied in the calculation of Q. Verify that assumptions about heat transfer are valid.
common_errors: Assuming conduction when radiation dominates
Ignoring mixed modes of heat transfer

rules.title: Account for Non-Ideal Gas Behavior
rules.description: For non-ideal gases, ensure that deviations from ideal gas behavior are considered in thermodynamic calculations.
rules.check_logic: Verify if corrections for non-ideal gas behavior (e.g., van der Waals equation) are applied when necessary. Ensure that ideal gas assumptions are not incorrectly used.
common_errors: Using ideal gas law for non-ideal gases
Ignoring intermolecular forces and finite molecular volume

rules.title: Apply Fourier's Law for Heat Conduction
rules.description: Fourier's Law states that the heat transfer rate (q) through a material is proportional to the temperature gradient and is given by q = -k * A * (dT/dx), where k is the thermal conductivity, A is the cross-sectional area, and dT/dx is the temperature gradient. This applies to steady-state, one-dimensional heat conduction.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the heat transfer rate is computed using q = -k * A * (dT/dx), that k, A, and dT/dx are correctly defined, and that the negative sign is used to indicate heat flows from high to low temperature.
common_errors: Incorrect sign: forgetting the negative sign indicating heat flows from high to low temperature.
Using incorrect or inconsistent units for thermal conductivity (k).
Forgetting to account for the cross-sectional area (A).
Misinterpreting the temperature gradient direction.

rules.title: Apply Newton's Law of Cooling for Convection
rules.description: Newton's Law of Cooling states that the convective heat transfer rate (q) is proportional to the temperature difference between the surface and the surrounding fluid: q = h * A * (T_surface - T_fluid), where h is the convective heat transfer coefficient, A is the surface area, and T_surface/T_fluid are the temperatures of the surface and fluid, respectively.
rules.check_logic: Ensure q is calculated using q = h * A * (T_surface - T_fluid), that all variables are correctly defined and evaluated, and that the temperature difference is calculated with the correct sign.
common_errors: Omitting the surface area (A) in the formula.
Using inconsistent units for the convective heat transfer coefficient (h).
Incorrectly calculating the temperature difference (e.g., wrong sign).
Applying the law when fluid motion or convection is not present.

rules.title: Apply Stefan-Boltzmann Law for Radiation
rules.description: The Stefan-Boltzmann Law states that the radiative heat transfer rate (q) from a surface is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature: q = ε * σ * A * (T_surface^4 - T_surroundings^4), where ε is the emissivity, σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, A is the surface area, and T_surface/T_surroundings are absolute temperatures (in Kelvin).
rules.check_logic: Verify that q is calculated using q = ε * σ * A * (T_surface^4 - T_surroundings^4), that temperatures are in Kelvin, and that emissivity (ε) is correctly applied.
common_errors: Forgetting to convert temperatures to Kelvin.
Mistaking emissivity (ε) as 1 when it's not explicitly stated.
Incorrectly raising temperatures to the fourth power.
Ignoring the surface area (A) in the calculation.

rules.title: Use Thermal Resistance Networks for Composite Systems
rules.description: In steady-state heat conduction across composite systems, the equivalent thermal resistance can be used to simplify the calculation. For series systems, R_eq = R1 + R2 + ...; for parallel systems, 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + .... Thermal resistance is defined as R = L/(k*A), where L is the material thickness.
rules.check_logic: Ensure thermal resistance is calculated correctly for series or parallel systems, combined appropriately to find the equivalent resistance, and that all layers or paths in the composite system are considered.
common_errors: Adding thermal resistances incorrectly for parallel configurations.
Using incorrect expressions for thermal resistance (e.g., forgetting the A term).
Mixing up series and parallel configurations.
Not considering all layers or paths in the composite system.

rules.title: Use Correct Sign Conventions for Heat Flow
rules.description: Heat flow is typically considered positive when it flows into a system and negative when it flows out. The chosen sign convention must remain consistent throughout the problem.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the sign convention for heat flow is consistently applied across all calculations and matches the physical scenario.
common_errors: Inconsistently assigning heat flow as positive or negative.
Forgetting to account for the chosen sign convention in intermediate steps.
Reversing the sign of heat flow in composite systems.

rules.title: Check Validity Conditions for Heat Transfer Equations
rules.description: Heat transfer equations (conduction, convection, radiation) have specific conditions for validity. Fourier's Law requires steady-state conduction, Newton's Law of Cooling assumes convective heat transfer, and Stefan-Boltzmann Law applies to radiative heat transfer in the absence of significant convection or conduction.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the heat transfer equation used is valid for the given physical conditions (e.g., steady state, type of heat transfer mechanism, absence of dominating alternate mechanisms).
common_errors: Using Fourier's Law when the system is not in steady state.
Applying Newton's Law of Cooling in the absence of fluid convection.
Using the Stefan-Boltzmann Law when conduction or convection dominates the heat transfer.

rules.title: Ensure Dimensional Consistency in Heat Transfer Equations
rules.description: Each term in the heat transfer equations must have consistent units. For example, in q = -k * A * (dT/dx), the units of q must match the product of k, A, and dT/dx.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all terms in the heat transfer equations have consistent units (e.g., energy/time or power) and that unit conversions are correctly applied.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for thermal conductivity (e.g., W/mK vs. W/cmK).
Neglecting to convert area or length units to match the desired unit system.
Incorrectly converting temperature gradients (e.g., Celsius per meter vs. Kelvin per meter).

rules.title: Apply Correct Boundary Conditions
rules.description: Heat transfer problems often involve specific boundary conditions, such as constant temperature, constant heat flux, or convection at the boundary. These must be correctly incorporated into the solution.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the boundary conditions are correctly applied, match the physical scenario, and are consistently used in solving the heat transfer equations.
common_errors: Misinterpreting or omitting boundary conditions.
Incorrectly applying a constant heat flux boundary condition.
Failing to match boundary conditions with the physical scenario (e.g., mixing convection and insulation).

rules.title: Account for Transient Heat Transfer
rules.description: In non-steady-state heat transfer, the temperature changes with time and must be modeled using transient heat transfer equations, such as the heat diffusion equation or lumped capacitance method.
rules.check_logic: Verify that transient heat transfer equations are used when the system is not in steady state and that initial and boundary conditions are correctly applied.
common_errors: Using steady-state equations for transient problems.
Ignoring initial conditions or time-dependent boundary conditions.
Incorrectly applying the lumped capacitance method when Biot number is not small.

topics.name: Work Done by Gases and PV Diagrams

rules.title: Verify work done using W = ∫PdV
rules.description: The work done by a gas in a thermodynamic process is calculated as the integral of pressure with respect to volume (W = ∫PdV). This equation applies when pressure is a function of volume or is constant during a process.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the work done is calculated as W = ∫P(V)dV when pressure depends on volume, or W = P * ΔV when pressure is constant. Verify that correct integration limits are used in each case.
common_errors: Using incorrect limits for the volume integral.
Assuming constant pressure in processes where pressure varies.
Neglecting the integral when pressure is not constant.

rules.title: Check sign convention for work done by the gas
rules.description: The sign convention for work in thermodynamics states that work done by the gas on the surroundings is positive, while work done on the gas is negative. This is crucial for correctly interpreting PV diagrams.
rules.check_logic: Verify that work is positive when the gas expands (ΔV > 0) and negative when the gas compresses (ΔV < 0). Confirm the correct application of sign conventions in calculations.
common_errors: Reversing the sign convention for expansion and compression.
Confusing work done by the gas with work done on the gas.

rules.title: Ensure work corresponds to area under PV curve
rules.description: On a PV diagram, the work done by the gas during a process is represented by the area under the curve between the initial and final volumes.
rules.check_logic: Check if the calculated work matches the geometrical area under the PV curve for the given process. Confirm correct interpretation of the curve's shape and limits.
common_errors: Incorrectly calculating area under the curve (e.g., forgetting to account for curve shape).
Using wrong limits for the area calculation.
Failing to include contributions from all segments of a multi-step process.

rules.title: Verify dimensional consistency of work done
rules.description: The work done by a gas has the units of energy (e.g., joules in SI units). This arises because pressure has units of force per unit area, and volume has units of length cubed.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the product of pressure (P, in Pa) and volume change (ΔV, in m³) has the resulting unit of energy (J). Verify that calculations involve consistent units.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for pressure or volume.
Neglecting to convert pressure or volume into consistent units before multiplication.

rules.title: Validate work done in isothermal processes
rules.description: For an isothermal process (constant temperature, ideal gas), the work done is W = nRT ln(V_f / V_i), where n is the number of moles, R is the ideal gas constant, T is the temperature, and V_f and V_i are the final and initial volumes.
rules.check_logic: Check if the work is calculated using W = nRT ln(V_f / V_i) for isothermal processes and ensure temperature remains constant throughout. Validate the formula usage and volume ratio order.
common_errors: Using incorrect formula for work in isothermal processes.
Not verifying that temperature remains constant.
Using incorrect limits for volume ratio (e.g., V_f / V_i).

rules.title: Validate work done in adiabatic processes
rules.description: For an adiabatic process (no heat exchange), the work done is related to the pressure, volume, and specific heat ratio (γ). The formula is W = (P_fV_f - P_iV_i) / (1 - γ) or equivalent forms.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the correct formula for work in adiabatic processes is used and verify that Q = 0 (no heat transfer). Confirm correct use of the specific heat ratio γ.
common_errors: Using the wrong formula for adiabatic work.
Failing to check that the process is adiabatic (Q ≠ 0).
Incorrectly applying γ (specific heat ratio) for the gas.

rules.title: Ensure net work done in a cyclic process equals enclosed area
rules.description: In a cyclic process (closed loop on a PV diagram), the net work done by the gas is equal to the area enclosed by the loop, with the sign depending on the direction of the cycle (clockwise or counterclockwise).
rules.check_logic: Check if the net work matches the geometrical area enclosed by the cycle and verify the direction of the cycle is correctly interpreted (clockwise = positive, counterclockwise = negative). Ensure proper identification of cycle direction in problem context.
common_errors: Incorrectly calculating the enclosed area.
Failing to account for the direction of the loop (clockwise = positive, counterclockwise = negative).
Mixing up processes within the cycle.

rules.title: Verify boundary conditions for work calculations
rules.description: Boundary conditions such as initial and final volumes, pressures, or temperatures must be consistent with the given process to correctly calculate work.
rules.check_logic: Ensure all initial and final state variables used in work calculations match the problem statement or given PV diagram. Validate state conditions are checked and consistent.
common_errors: Using incorrect or inconsistent boundary conditions.
Failing to check for state variable consistency in multi-step processes.
Neglecting changes in state variables due to heat exchange or additional forces.

rules.title: Verify PV = nRT for Isothermal Process
rules.description: During an isothermal process, the temperature remains constant. The ideal gas law (PV = nRT) is used to relate pressure, volume, and amount of substance with the constant temperature.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the temperature is constant throughout the process. Verify that PV = nRT holds for both the initial and final states, using Kelvin for the temperature.
common_errors: Incorrect usage of ideal gas law when temperature is not constant.
Forgetting to convert temperatures to Kelvin.
Not using amount of substance in moles.

rules.title: Ensure PV^γ = constant for Adiabatic Process
rules.description: In an adiabatic process, no heat exchange occurs. The equation PV^γ = constant should be used, where γ is the heat capacity ratio (Cp/Cv).
rules.check_logic: Verify that no heat transfer occurs (Q=0) and check that PV^γ = constant throughout the process.
common_errors: Miscalculation of γ (Cp/Cv) or using incorrect gas properties.
Not verifying the condition of no heat exchange.
Inappropriate use of PV = nRT without considering adiabatic conditions.

rules.title: Apply First Law of Thermodynamics Correctly
rules.description: The first law entails energy conservation, expressed as ΔU = Q - W, where ΔU is the change in internal energy, Q is heat added to the system, and W is the work done by the system.
rules.check_logic: Calculate ΔU using ΔU = Q - W, identifying Q and W based on the process type. Ensure correct sign conventions are used.
common_errors: Not distinguishing between work done on and by the system.
Misinterpretation of sign conventions for heat and work.
Omitting internal energy change calculation.

rules.title: Check Sign Conventions for Work and Heat
rules.description: Sign conventions dictate that heat (Q) added to the system is positive, and work (W) done by the system is positive according to classical convention.
rules.check_logic: Confirm correct sign assignment for heat and work in process equations.
common_errors: Confusing sign conventions between different textbooks or resources.
Incorrectly assigning signs for exothermic and endothermic reactions.
Ignoring sign conventions in calculations leading to erroneous energy balance.

rules.title: Validate Geometric Volume Constraints
rules.description: Certain processes involve geometric constraints. Verify volume changes conform to system constraints such as constant volume (isochoric) or variable volume.
rules.check_logic: Ensure volume changes reflect geometric constraints. Verify appropriately for fixed or variable volume processes.
common_errors: Not accounting for fixed volume in isochoric processes.
Incorrectly assuming volume change when it is geometrically constrained.
Neglecting compatibility with experimental or real-world constraints.

rules.title: Ensure Dimensional Consistency and Unit Use
rules.description: Dimensional consistency is critical. All equations must maintain unit consistency. Variables must be expressed in compatible units, e.g., temperatures in Kelvin, volumes in m³, pressure in Pa.
rules.check_logic: Check equations for dimensional consistency and confirm unit conversions where necessary.
common_errors: Mixing units (e.g., Celsius with Kelvin, atm with Pa).
Neglecting unit conversions leading to incorrect results.
Confusing energy units like joules, calories, etc.

rules.title: Assess Validity of Reversible Process Assumption
rules.description: Reversible process assumptions require specific conditions. Real-world processes often deviate from this ideal. Validate applicability before enforcement.
rules.check_logic: Ensure assumptions of reversibility align with process conditions, such as infinitesimally slow change and lack of energy dissipation.
common_errors: Incorrectly applying reversible process assumptions to irreversible scenarios.
Ignoring effects like friction or turbulence that negate reversibility.
Assuming perfect insulation in adiabatic processes.

rules.title: Verify Positive Entropy Change for Irreversible Processes
rules.description: According to the second law of thermodynamics, entropy change must be greater than zero for irreversible processes.
rules.check_logic: If a process is identified as irreversible, verify that entropy change (ΔS) > 0. For reversible processes, ΔS = 0.
common_errors: Incorrectly calculating ΔS = 0 for irreversible processes
Using ΔS < 0 for spontaneous processes
Failing to distinguish between reversible and irreversible processes

rules.title: Entropy Dimensional Consistency
rules.description: Entropy must have the dimension of energy per temperature, typically joules per kelvin (J/K).
rules.check_logic: Ensure calculated entropy is expressed in units of J/K and verify dimensional consistency in calculations.
common_errors: Using incorrect units like J or K
Mixing units of power (Watts) with entropy
Failing to convert units properly in intermediate steps

rules.title: Confirm Maximum Efficiency for Carnot Cycle
rules.description: The efficiency of any cyclic heat engine cannot be greater than that of a Carnot cycle operating between the same high and low temperature reservoirs.
rules.check_logic: If a heat engine is compared against a Carnot engine, verify that η_engine ≤ η_Carnot = 1 - T_cold/T_hot, where temperatures are in absolute scale (Kelvin).
common_errors: Calculating η_engine > η_Carnot
Misidentifying T_cold and T_hot temperatures
Using temperatures in Celsius instead of Kelvin

rules.title: Adhere to Entropy Sign Convention
rules.description: The entropy change is positive for heat absorption and negative for heat rejection.
rules.check_logic: In processes involving heat transfer, ensure entropy change aligns with Q/T, where Q is heat absorbed (positive) or rejected (negative), and T is the absolute temperature.
common_errors: Confusing the sign of entropy change for heat absorbed vs. rejected
Neglecting to change sign when transitioning from absorption to rejection
Using incorrect temperature values for T

rules.title: Validate Boltzmann's Entropy Formula Application
rules.description: Boltzmann's entropy formula S = k ln(Ω) applies to systems in statistical equilibrium with a well-defined number of microstates.
rules.check_logic: Ensure applicability of S = k ln(Ω) by verifying that the system is in equilibrium, Ω (number of microstates) is well-defined, and k is Boltzmann's constant.
common_errors: Applying Boltzmann's formula to non-equilibrium systems
Miscalculating Ω or ignoring its determination
Using incorrect value for Boltzmann's constant

rules.title: Confirm Zero Entropy Change in Adiabatic Processes
rules.description: In adiabatic processes without irreversibilities, the change in entropy should be zero.
rules.check_logic: Check that for adiabatic processes (no heat exchange), ΔS = 0 unless internal irreversibilities are present. If irreversibilities exist, verify ΔS > 0.
common_errors: Assuming ΔS ≠ 0 for perfect adiabatic processes
Failing to identify presence of irreversibilities
Misinterpreting adiabatic processes as isothermal

rules.title: Assess Entropy Conservation in Isothermal Conditions
rules.description: During isothermal reversible processes, entropy changes are balanced such that ΔS_total = 0 for the system and surroundings.
rules.check_logic: Ensure ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings = 0 during a reversible isothermal process. Verify that heat transfer is consistent with Q/T for both system and surroundings.
common_errors: Ignoring entropy changes in surroundings during isothermal balancing
Misleading zero entropy system change as total entropy conservation
Failing to account for reversibility conditions

rules.title: Check Validity Conditions: Second Law Applications
rules.description: The second law applies universally for entropy considerations but is specifically valid for macroscopic systems in classical regimes. It cannot distinguish between microscopic fluctuations.
rules.check_logic: Verify application to classical, macroscopic systems and ensure that anomalies due to quantum or microscopic factors are not wrongly interpreted by the second law.
common_errors: Misapplication to quantum scale systems
Ignoring classical regime requirements in justification
Overlooking microscopic fluctuations in small systems

rules.title: Verify Entropy Behavior at Extremes
rules.description: Entropy approaches zero as temperature approaches absolute zero, consistent with the third law of thermodynamics.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that entropy calculations reflect S → 0 as T → 0 for perfect crystalline substances, and verify that entropy does not decrease below zero.
common_errors: Violating the third law by allowing negative entropy
Failing to account for residual entropy in non-perfect crystals
Incorrectly extrapolating entropy behavior at low temperatures

rules.title: Apply Carnot Efficiency Formula
rules.description: The Carnot efficiency equation is used to calculate the maximum efficiency of a heat engine operating between two thermal reservoirs. It is given by η = 1 - (T_cold / T_hot), where T_cold and T_hot are the absolute temperatures of the cold and hot reservoirs, respectively.
rules.check_logic: Calculate η using η = 1 - (T_cold / T_hot). Ensure that temperatures are in Kelvin and T_hot > T_cold.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin for temperatures
Mixing up T_hot and T_cold
Incorrect subtraction or division order
Using negative temperatures without proper conversion

rules.title: Verify Reversible Process in Carnot Cycle
rules.description: A Carnot cycle consists of four reversible processes: two isothermal and two adiabatic. The cycle is hypothetically reversible, and real engines operating on Carnot principles should approach reversibility.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the process sequence is isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, adiabatic compression. Confirm that no heat exchange occurs during adiabatic processes and that heat exchange occurs only during isothermal processes.
common_errors: Failing to identify the correct sequence of processes
Mistaking any process as irreversible
Incorrectly labeling adiabatic processes as isothermal
Ignoring the reversibility assumption in calculations

rules.title: Check Temperature Units in Carnot Calculations
rules.description: Temperatures in thermodynamic calculations involving Carnot cycles must be expressed in absolute units (Kelvin). This ensures correct comparison and ratios in formulas.
rules.check_logic: Verify all temperatures are given in Kelvin before substitution into formulas. If temperatures are provided in Celsius, convert them to Kelvin using T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.
common_errors: Using Celsius or Fahrenheit for temperature inputs
Ignoring unit conversion entirely
Wrong conversion from Celsius to Kelvin
Failing to check for negative temperatures in Celsius

rules.title: Validate Carnot Cycle Assumptions with Ideal Gas
rules.description: Carnot engines often assume gases behave ideally in the cycle. This requires conditions where the gas's behavior approximates the ideal gas law closely.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the problem context or conditions denote ideal gas behavior or provide necessary conditions such as low pressure and high temperature. Verify that the ideal gas law (PV = nRT) is applicable.
common_errors: Assuming ideal behavior when conditions don't support it
Using real gas equations without context clarity
Failing to match conditions with equation assumptions
Ignoring deviations from ideal gas behavior at high pressures or low temperatures

rules.title: Efficiency Limitation Recognition
rules.description: The Carnot efficiency represents the maximum efficiency limit for any heat engine operating between two temperatures. No real engine can surpass this efficiency.
rules.check_logic: Compare calculated engine efficiency with Carnot efficiency (η_c). Report if any real engine efficiency exceeds η_c. Ensure that η_c is calculated correctly using absolute temperatures.
common_errors: Claiming real engine efficiency exceeds Carnot limit
Neglecting the efficiency definition for non-Carnot engines
Misinterpreting efficiency calculations
Failing to account for irreversibilities in real engines

rules.title: Ensure Work Done Calculations in Adiabatic Processes
rules.description: In adiabatic processes of a Carnot cycle, work done relies on pressure and volume changes, with no heat exchange occurring.
rules.check_logic: Evaluate work done using adiabatic relations: W = μ(C_vm/T)*(V_initial/V_final)^(γ-1) where applicable. Confirm that Q = 0 for adiabatic processes.
common_errors: Confusing adiabatic with isochoric processes
Using heat transfer equations in adiabatic calculations
Incorrect exponent calculation involving adiabatic processes
Failing to verify that no heat is exchanged (Q = 0)

rules.title: Verify Net Power Output Calculation
rules.description: The net power output of a Carnot engine is calculated from the net work done in one complete cycle, considering all processes.
rules.check_logic: Calculate net work as W_net = Q_h - Q_c, where Q_h is heat input and Q_c is heat output. Ensure that Q_h > Q_c and that heat values are consistent with the first law of thermodynamics.
common_errors: Incorrectly adding rather than subtracting heats
Omitting work done calculations
Confusion between input and output heat quantities
Failing to check consistency with the first law of thermodynamics

rules.title: Constrain Cycle Path in P-V Diagram
rules.description: The Carnot cycle should accurately reflect its adiabatic and isothermal paths in a P-V diagram, depicting ideal process transitions.
rules.check_logic: Ensure diagram paths are correct: isothermal paths are horizontal while adiabatic paths should curve according to pressure-temperature changes. Verify that transitions between processes are smooth and consistent with thermodynamic principles.
common_errors: Incorrectly labeling isothermal paths as vertical
Misrepresenting adiabatic curves with straight lines
Failing to respect process transitions accurately on diagrams
Ignoring the relationship between pressure, volume, and temperature in the diagram

rules.title: Verify Heat Transfer in Isothermal Processes
rules.description: During isothermal processes in the Carnot cycle, heat transfer occurs at constant temperature. The heat absorbed or released is related to the work done.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that Q = W for isothermal processes, where Q is the heat transferred and W is the work done. Verify that the temperature remains constant throughout the process.
common_errors: Failing to equate heat transfer to work done in isothermal processes
Assuming temperature changes during isothermal processes
Ignoring the relationship between heat transfer and work

rules.title: Verify the fundamental thermodynamic equations.
rules.description: Check the use of fundamental thermodynamic equations, such as the Helmholtz free energy (F = U - TS) and Gibbs free energy (G = H - TS). These equations connect internal energy, enthalpy, entropy, and temperature.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the expressions for F and G are correctly derived from internal energy (U) and enthalpy (H), and that temperature (T) and entropy (S) are correctly included with appropriate coefficients. Verify that the equations are dimensionally consistent and that all terms are properly labeled.
common_errors: Omitting the TS term in the equations.
Mislabeling variables (e.g., using H instead of U in Helmholtz free energy).
Incorrectly rearranging terms in the equations.

rules.title: Confirm correct sign conventions in thermodynamic potentials.
rules.description: In thermodynamics, positive work done by the system and heat added to the system are considered positive. Ensure that these conventions are consistently applied when using thermodynamic potentials.
rules.check_logic: Verify that work, heat, and other energy terms follow the sign conventions in derivations and calculations involving F or G. Ensure that the signs are consistent with the first and second laws of thermodynamics.
common_errors: Using the wrong sign for work done by or on the system.
Confusing heat absorbed with heat released and applying incorrect signs.
Incorrect sign application when relating F or G to system properties (e.g., pressure or temperature).

rules.title: Check partial derivatives of thermodynamic potentials.
rules.description: Thermodynamic potentials have specific relationships with system variables. For example, (∂F/∂V)_T = -P and (∂G/∂P)_T = V. These partial derivatives must be correctly applied when computing thermodynamic quantities.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the correct derivative relationships are used for the given potential and variable of interest. Ensure that the appropriate variable is held constant during differentiation and that the physical interpretation of the derivative is correct.
common_errors: Incorrect partial derivative relationships (e.g., swapping variables like pressure and volume).
Forgetting to hold the appropriate variable constant (e.g., temperature).
Using an incorrect thermodynamic potential for the derivative.

rules.title: Ensure dimensional and unit consistency in thermodynamic potentials.
rules.description: Thermodynamic potentials must have units of energy (e.g., Joules in the SI system). Ensure all terms in the equations have consistent dimensions and units.
rules.check_logic: Check that each term in F, G, and related expressions has the same dimensions, and that derived quantities (e.g., partial derivatives) are dimensionally consistent. Verify that unit conversions are correctly applied when switching between unit systems.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for temperature, entropy, or pressure.
Neglecting unit conversions when switching between systems (e.g., SI to CGS).
Combining terms with mismatched dimensions (e.g., mixing energy with pressure).

rules.title: Verify validity conditions for thermodynamic potentials.
rules.description: Helmholtz free energy is used in systems at constant temperature and volume, while Gibbs free energy applies to constant temperature and pressure. Ensure the conditions for applying each potential are explicitly stated and satisfied.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the problem specifies constant temperature and appropriate constraints (volume for F, pressure for G) before using the corresponding potential. Verify that the assumptions are explicitly stated in the problem setup.
common_errors: Using Helmholtz free energy in a system where pressure is not constant.
Applying Gibbs free energy to a system with varying temperature.
Neglecting to check if the required conditions are satisfied before proceeding.

rules.title: Check maximum work conditions for free energy changes.
rules.description: Helmholtz free energy (F) represents the maximum work extractable at constant temperature and volume. Gibbs free energy (G) represents the maximum non-expansion work at constant temperature and pressure.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the work extracted does not exceed the changes in F or G under the specified conditions. Ensure that the type of work (e.g., expansion or non-expansion) is correctly identified and that the appropriate potential is used.
common_errors: Calculating work exceeding the change in free energy.
Misinterpreting the type of work (e.g., expansion vs. non-expansion work).
Applying the wrong potential for the given constraints.

rules.title: Verify equilibrium conditions using thermodynamic potentials.
rules.description: At equilibrium, thermodynamic potentials reach their minimum values under the specified constraints (F for constant T and V, G for constant T and P). Check if this principle is correctly applied.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the potential is minimized at equilibrium, and that the conditions for equilibrium (e.g., ∂F/∂V = 0 or ∂G/∂P = 0) are satisfied. Verify that higher-order derivatives are used to confirm stability when necessary.
common_errors: Failing to check for minimum potential values at equilibrium.
Using the wrong thermodynamic potential for the given constraints.
Ignoring higher-order derivatives to confirm stability.

rules.title: Verify Legendre transforms between thermodynamic potentials.
rules.description: Thermodynamic potentials are related via Legendre transforms. For example, G = F + PV. Ensure such transformations are correctly executed and account for all variables.
rules.check_logic: Check that the Legendre transform equations are correctly applied and that all terms are included with proper signs. Verify that the starting potential and the transformed potential are consistent with the problem's constraints.
common_errors: Forgetting to include PV or TS terms in the transformation.
Incorrect sign convention in Legendre transforms.
Using an incorrect thermodynamic potential as the starting point.

rules.title: Verify stability conditions for thermodynamic potentials.
rules.description: Thermodynamic stability requires that the second derivatives of potentials satisfy specific conditions. For example, (∂²F/∂V²)_T > 0 ensures stability at constant temperature and volume.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the second derivatives of the potential are consistent with stability criteria. Ensure that the appropriate variables are held constant during differentiation.
common_errors: Neglecting to check second derivatives for stability.
Using incorrect stability criteria for the given potential.
Failing to hold the appropriate variables constant during differentiation.

rules.title: Verify correct partial derivative relationships in Maxwell's relations
rules.description: Maxwell's relations originate from the symmetry of second derivatives in thermodynamic potentials. Ensure that the correct partial derivatives are used, such as (∂T/∂V)_S = -(∂P/∂S)_V.
rules.check_logic: Check if the second mixed partial derivatives of the thermodynamic potentials are correctly equated. For example, verify that (∂²G/∂T∂P) = (∂²G/∂P∂T). Ensure that the variables and signs are consistent with the specific Maxwell relation being used.
common_errors: Incorrect variable pairings (e.g., swapping T and S when differentiating)
Omitting the minus sign in some relations
Using the wrong thermodynamic potential for the given variables

rules.title: Ensure thermodynamic equilibrium for Maxwell's relations application
rules.description: Maxwell's relations are derived under the assumption of thermodynamic equilibrium. Check if the system satisfies equilibrium conditions, such as constant temperature, pressure, or no net heat flow.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the problem statement explicitly mentions thermodynamic equilibrium or conditions implying equilibrium (e.g., constant T, P, or volume). Ensure that transient or irreversible processes are not mistakenly analyzed using Maxwell's relations.
common_errors: Applying Maxwell's relations to systems not in equilibrium
Ignoring transient or irreversible processes

rules.title: Check dimension/unit consistency in Maxwell's relations
rules.description: Maxwell's relations involve quantities like temperature (T), entropy (S), pressure (P), volume (V), and energy (E). Ensure that the units or dimensions of derivatives match (e.g., (∂T/∂V)_S has units of T/V).
rules.check_logic: Verify that the units of the partial derivatives are consistent with the definition of the thermodynamic state function. For example, (∂P/∂T)_V should have units of pressure/temperature. Ensure that unit conversions, if any, are handled correctly.
common_errors: Mismatch in units of variables during differentiation
Incorrectly handling unit conversion factors (e.g., for entropy in different units)

rules.title: Verify correct sign conventions in Maxwell's relations
rules.description: Sign conventions in thermodynamics are crucial. For example, entropy increases (+) when heat is added to the system, and work done by the system decreases energy (-).
rules.check_logic: Verify that negative signs are placed correctly in Maxwell's relations, such as - (∂P/∂S)_V or - (∂T/∂V)_S. Ensure that the sign conventions align with the physical interpretation of the thermodynamic quantities.
common_errors: Forgetting the negative sign in the relation
Reversing the sign of work or entropy changes

rules.title: Ensure compatibility of thermodynamic potentials with chosen Maxwell relation
rules.description: Maxwell's relations are derived from specific thermodynamic potentials (U, H, G, A). Verify that the chosen relation corresponds to the correct potential.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the thermodynamic potential used matches the relation. For example, (∂S/∂V)_T is derived from Helmholtz free energy (A). Ensure that the potential is correctly identified based on the variables involved.
common_errors: Using Gibbs free energy (G) instead of Helmholtz free energy (A)
Applying the wrong potential to the given variable set

rules.title: Check if boundary conditions are consistent with Maxwell's relations
rules.description: Maxwell's relations often involve fixed variables (e.g., constant T, P, or V). Ensure the problem statement specifies these conditions for the relation to hold.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the fixed variables (e.g., constant T or V) are explicitly stated or implied in the problem. Ensure that the chosen Maxwell relation corresponds to the specified boundary conditions.
common_errors: Applying the wrong Maxwell relation due to misunderstanding fixed variables
Omitting the constraint condition entirely

rules.title: Verify geometric constraints for volume-related Maxwell relations
rules.description: When using Maxwell's relations involving volume (V), ensure that the system has well-defined and physically meaningful geometric constraints (e.g., no negative volume).
rules.check_logic: Check that the volume is positive and finite, and physically plausible constraints (like incompressibility) are respected. Ensure that the geometric constraints are consistent with the thermodynamic assumptions.
common_errors: Allowing negative or zero volume in calculations
Neglecting imposed constraints like incompressibility or boundary limits

rules.title: Ensure statistical mechanics consistency in derivation of Maxwell's relations
rules.description: Maxwell's relations can be derived from statistical mechanics. Verify that the macroscopic thermodynamic quantities used (e.g., S, T, P) are consistent with the statistical interpretation (e.g., entropy from microstates).
rules.check_logic: Confirm the thermodynamic quantities align with their statistical definitions, such as S = k_B ln(Ω). Ensure that the Boltzmann constant (k_B) and other statistical parameters are used consistently.
common_errors: Misinterpreting entropy as heat instead of its statistical definition
Inconsistent use of Boltzmann constant (k_B) in units or calculations

rules.title: Verify numerical implementation of Maxwell's relations
rules.description: When Maxwell's relations are used in numerical calculations, ensure that the numerical methods (e.g., finite differences) are implemented correctly.
rules.check_logic: Verify that numerical approximations of derivatives (e.g., ∂P/∂T) are consistent with the analytical expressions. Check for proper handling of numerical precision and rounding errors.
common_errors: Incorrect numerical differentiation methods
Ignoring numerical precision issues leading to significant errors

rules.title: Verify Ideal Gas Law Application
rules.description: The Ideal Gas Law PV = nRT relates pressure (P), volume (V), number of moles (n), and temperature (T). It applies to ideal gases, which are assumed to have perfectly elastic collisions and negligible volume occupied by the gas particles.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the problem conditions specify an ideal gas, often monoatomic and low-pressure conditions. Check if all the variables in PV = nRT are accounted for, and verify units: P in pascal, V in cubic meters, n in moles, R = 8.314 J/mol·K, and T in Kelvin.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin for temperature
Incorrect unit conversion for pressure or volume
Omitting gas constant R
Confusion between atmospheric pressure and pressure in pascal

rules.title: Calculate Average Kinetic Energy per Molecule
rules.description: Average kinetic energy per molecule in an ideal gas is given by (3/2)kT, where k is Boltzmann's constant and T is absolute temperature.
rules.check_logic: Verify that temperature is expressed in Kelvin and k is correctly used as 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K. Check dimensional consistency for energy output in joules.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin
Misplacement of 3/2 factor in kinetic energy calculation
Incorrect value or units for Boltzmann's constant

rules.title: Verify Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution Assumptions
rules.description: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution describes the distribution of speeds of particles in a gas at a given temperature. It assumes non-interacting and identical particles.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the system being analyzed is monoatomic and exhibits classical behavior, no quantum effects. This distribution is valid for a large number of particles and at thermal equilibrium.
common_errors: Incorrectly applying Maxwell-Boltzmann to quantum or interacting systems
Calculations outside validity range

rules.title: Verify Mean Free Path Calculation
rules.description: Mean free path is the average distance traveled by a molecule between collisions. Use the formula λ = kT / (sqrt(2) * π * d^2 * P), where d is the molecular diameter.
rules.check_logic: Check units: λ in meters, diameter d in meters, pressure P in pascal, temperature T in Kelvin. Ensure conditions describe an ideal gas scenario.
common_errors: Incorrect diameter units
Failing to include sqrt(2) factor
Using non-ideal gas conditions
Incorrect conditions for low density or high temperature cases

rules.title: Relate Temperature to Internal Energy
rules.description: For a monoatomic ideal gas, internal energy U is proportional to temperature T as U = (3/2)nRT. This applies only to monoatomic gases.
rules.check_logic: Confirm the gas type is monoatomic and temperature is clearly defined in Kelvin. Ensure correct usage of mole quantity n and gas constant R.
common_errors: Applying relation to non-monoatomic gases
Misinterpretation of temperature scale
Neglecting mole count or incorrect R
Incorrect conditions for systems at very high or low temperatures

rules.title: Validate Degrees of Freedom in Energy Distribution
rules.description: Equipartition theorem states that each degree of freedom contributes (1/2)kT to the energy for ideal gases.
rules.check_logic: Ensure degrees of freedom are correctly determined based on molecular structure (e.g., 3 translational for monoatomic gases).
common_errors: Incorrect count of degrees of freedom
Misapplication of (1/2)kT per degree of freedom
Wrong assumption for polyatomic gases
Not accounting for rotational and vibrational degrees in complex molecules

rules.title: Check Dimensional Consistency in Calculations
rules.description: All calculated dimensions and units for derived quantities from kinetic theory must be consistent (e.g., pressure in pascal, volume in m^3, temperature in Kelvin).
rules.check_logic: Review each equation and result for dimensional consistency using SI units. Flag conversion errors for immediate correction.
common_errors: Mixing units (e.g., liters vs m^3 for volume)
Temperature in Celsius leading to inconsistent dimensions
Pressure in atm instead of pascal without conversion
Neglecting standard conditions definitions, leading to confusion

rules.title: Verify Thermal Boundary Conditions
rules.description: Ensure that thermal boundary conditions are properly defined and adhered to, concerning ideal and real gas behaviors.
rules.check_logic: Identify whether boundary conditions for pressure, volume, and temperature are specified and align with thermodynamic assumptions for ideal gases.
common_errors: Ignoring effects of container materials affecting thermal boundaries
Assuming perfectly insulated systems without specification
Omitting consideration of external temperature fluctuations

topics.name: Ideal Gas Law and Real Gas Behavior

rules.title: Verify Ideal Gas Law Formulation
rules.description: The ideal gas law is expressed as PV = nRT, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is the number of moles, R is the universal gas constant, and T is temperature in kelvins. This relationship applies to ideal gases under standard conditions.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the equation is explicitly written as PV = nRT with all variables correctly assigned and units suitable for the context.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for R (e.g., J/mol·K with P in atm)
Failure to convert temperature to kelvins
Misplacing or misinterpreting variables within the equation

rules.title: Ensure Temperature is in Kelvins
rules.description: The ideal gas law requires the absolute temperature in kelvins. Celsius or Fahrenheit must be converted to kelvins using T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the temperature has been converted to kelvins before using it in the ideal gas equation and note any errors in conversion.
common_errors: Using Celsius or Fahrenheit directly in calculations
Forgetting to add 273.15 when converting from Celsius to kelvins

rules.title: Check Dimensional Consistency of Ideal Gas Law
rules.description: Each term in the ideal gas law must have consistent units. For example, P in Pascals, V in cubic meters, n in moles, T in kelvins, and R in J/(mol·K).
rules.check_logic: Ensure that units for each variable are coherent and consistent throughout calculations, especially when mixing English and SI units.
common_errors: Mixing units that are not compatible (e.g., atm for pressure and cubic meters for volume)
Using non-SI units without proper conversion

rules.title: Check Validity of Ideal Gas Law Assumptions
rules.description: The ideal gas law assumes negligible intermolecular forces and that gas particles occupy no volume. It is valid at low pressures and high temperatures where these assumptions are close.
rules.check_logic: Evaluate the pressure and temperature conditions of the problem and determine the appropriateness of applying the ideal gas law.
common_errors: Applying the ideal gas law to high-pressure or low-temperature scenarios
Ignoring intermolecular forces in dense gases

rules.title: Consider Real Gas Corrections (Van der Waals Equation)
rules.description: For real gases, the Van der Waals equation (P + a(n/V)^2)(V - nb) = nRT accounts for intermolecular forces and finite particle volume. Use this equation under non-ideal conditions.
rules.check_logic: Determine if the problem presents conditions that require accounting for real gas behavior, notably at high pressure or low temperature.
common_errors: Using the ideal gas law when real gas behavior is significant
Neglecting correction terms a and b

rules.title: Verify Work Sign Convention in Gas Expansion/Compression
rules.description: When a gas expands, work is done by the gas, and W is positive. When compressed, work is done on the gas, and W is negative.
rules.check_logic: Confirm the direction of work based on volume changes to apply correct sign convention, ensuring consistency with the first law of thermodynamics.
common_errors: Flipping the sign of work
Inconsistencies in work calculations within the context of ΔU = Q - W

rules.title: Verify Constraints for Isothermal, Isobaric, Isochoric, and Adiabatic Processes
rules.description: Verify fixed or zero values for properties specific to these processes: T constant for isothermal, P constant for isobaric, V constant for isochoric, and Q = 0 for adiabatic process.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the correct variable is being treated according to the type of process and verify constraints are appropriately applied.
common_errors: Not maintaining constant temperature in isothermal processes
Neglecting Q = 0 in adiabatic processes
Failing to maintain P or V constant in isobaric or isochoric processes

rules.title: Check Molar Mass and Mass-Volume Conversions
rules.description: Verify correct calculation of mole number using n = m/M, where m is mass and M is molar mass, important for correct use in gas law equations.
rules.check_logic: Confirm the mass and volume conversions, ensuring the molar mass is accurate and correctly used to convert mass to moles.
common_errors: Omitting division of mass by molar mass
Utilizing incorrect molar mass figures

rules.title: Check Entropy Change Calculations in Thermodynamic Processes
rules.description: Ensure correct assessment of entropy changes (ΔS) based on process type and whether the gas is ideal or real.
rules.check_logic: Evaluate entropy changes considering the process specifics, such as temperature changes and phase transitions, applicable to ideal and real gas scenarios.
common_errors: Ignoring factors impacting entropy change
Assuming no entropy change during irreversible processes without proper justification

rules.title: Ensure correctness of Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution equation
rules.description: The Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution is given by f(v) = 4π * (m / 2πkT)^(3/2) * v^2 * exp(-mv^2 / 2kT). This equation describes the probability density of molecular speeds in an ideal gas at thermal equilibrium. It applies only to ideal gases where intermolecular interactions are negligible.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the provided equation matches the standard form, including all terms, exponents, and the exponential factor. Ensure that the equation is dimensionally consistent.
common_errors: Omitting the factor of 4π in the equation
Incorrect exponent in the term (m / 2πkT)
Forgetting the v^2 term in the equation
Misplacing or misinterpreting the exponential factor (-mv^2 / 2kT)

rules.title: Check unit consistency in Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
rules.description: In the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution, ensure that the units are consistent: m should be in kg, k (Boltzmann constant) in J/K, T in K, and v in m/s. The overall units of f(v) should be 1/(m/s), as it's a probability density over speed.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the units of each term in the equation are consistent and that f(v) has units of 1/(m/s). Ensure that all constants and variables are expressed in SI units.
common_errors: Mixing units of mass (e.g., using grams instead of kilograms)
Using incorrect units for Boltzmann constant (e.g., not converting to J/K)
Forgetting to ensure that temperature is in Kelvin

rules.title: Ensure correct calculation of mean speed
rules.description: The mean speed for the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is given by ⟨v⟩ = sqrt(8kT / πm). This is derived by integrating the speed distribution function. It applies only to ideal gases in thermal equilibrium.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the mean speed is calculated using ⟨v⟩ = sqrt(8kT / πm) and that all terms are correctly substituted. Ensure that the units of the result are consistent with m/s.
common_errors: Incorrect formula for mean speed (e.g., using root-mean-square speed instead)
Forgetting the factor of sqrt(8/π)
Not substituting temperature or mass correctly into the formula

rules.title: Ensure correct calculation of root-mean-square (RMS) speed
rules.description: The root-mean-square speed in the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is given by v_rms = sqrt(3kT / m). This represents the square root of the average of the speed squared and applies only to ideal gases in thermal equilibrium.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the RMS speed is calculated using v_rms = sqrt(3kT / m) and that all terms are correctly substituted. Ensure that the units of the result are consistent with m/s.
common_errors: Confusing RMS speed with mean speed or most probable speed
Forgetting the factor of sqrt(3)
Misplacing variables (e.g., swapping m and kT)

rules.title: Ensure correct calculation of most probable speed
rules.description: The most probable speed in the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is given by v_mp = sqrt(2kT / m). This is the speed at which the probability density f(v) is maximized. It applies only to ideal gases in thermal equilibrium.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the most probable speed is calculated using v_mp = sqrt(2kT / m) and that all terms are correctly substituted. Ensure that the units of the result are consistent with m/s.
common_errors: Using incorrect formula for v_mp (e.g., confusing it with mean or RMS speed)
Forgetting the factor of sqrt(2)
Not verifying the maximization condition for f(v)

rules.title: Check validity conditions for Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
rules.description: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution applies only to ideal gases in thermal equilibrium. It assumes negligible intermolecular interactions, classical mechanics (non-relativistic speeds), and a continuous spectrum of molecular speeds.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the problem specifies an ideal gas at thermal equilibrium and that the given conditions satisfy classical mechanics (v << c). Ensure that the system is not quantum mechanical (e.g., Bose-Einstein or Fermi-Dirac statistics).
common_errors: Applying Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution to non-ideal gases
Assuming the distribution holds at relativistic speeds (v ~ c)
Using the distribution for quantum systems (e.g., Bose-Einstein or Fermi-Dirac statistics)

rules.title: Perform dimensional analysis for Maxwell-Boltzmann-related calculations
rules.description: All derived quantities from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution — such as mean speed, RMS speed, and most probable speed — must have the correct dimensional consistency. The derived speed formulae must have units of m/s.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the derived expressions for speed (mean, RMS, most probable) yield units of m/s, and that all intermediate terms are dimensionally consistent. Verify that constants like k and m are expressed in SI units.
common_errors: Incorrect units in intermediate calculations (e.g., using temperature in Celsius instead of Kelvin)
Not verifying the dimensions of the Boltzmann constant
Forgetting to ensure consistent units for mass and speed

rules.title: Check normalization of Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
rules.description: The Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution must integrate over all speeds to 1 (normalization).
rules.check_logic: Verify that the distribution integrates to 1 over all speeds. Ensure that the integration limits are correct and that the normalization constant is properly included.
common_errors: Forgetting to normalize the distribution
Incorrect integration limits for verifying normalization
Neglecting the normalization constant in the equation

rules.title: Verify peak of Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
rules.description: The Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution should peak at the most probable speed (v_mp).
rules.check_logic: Verify that the derivative of the distribution function f(v) with respect to v is zero at v = v_mp, confirming that the peak occurs at the most probable speed.
common_errors: Not verifying the derivative condition for the peak
Incorrect calculation of the most probable speed
Assuming the peak occurs at mean or RMS speed instead of v_mp

rules.title: Apply Clausius-Clapeyron Equation
rules.description: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation describes the slope of the phase boundary in a pressure-temperature diagram for phase transitions. It applies when the transition is between phases in equilibrium with no external work done.
rules.check_logic: Verify the equation dP/dT = L/TV, where L is the latent heat and V is the change in volume, under equilibrium conditions.
common_errors: Incorrect differentiation of pressure with respect to temperature
Miscalculation of latent heat and volume change
Not considering the equilibrium condition

rules.title: Check units of latent heat
rules.description: Latent heat should be expressed in units consistent with energy per mass (e.g., J/kg or cal/g). Dimensional consistency is crucial for correct calculations.
rules.check_logic: Ensure latent heat is given as energy per unit mass and consistently convert units where needed.
common_errors: Using energy units like joules without per mass unit
Incorrect conversion between calories and joules or between grams and kilograms
Ignoring units during calculation

rules.title: Verify entropy change during phase transition
rules.description: Entropy change should be calculated as S = L/T during a phase transition where the system is in thermal equilibrium.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the calculated S matches L/T, verifying that L is in proper energy units and T is in Kelvin.
common_errors: Wrong temperature unit; only Kelvin should be used
Neglecting the equilibrium condition resulting in incorrect entropy values
Incorrect calculations leading to negative entropy changes
